acts.title: THE APPRAISAL
acts.goal: Land on the headland, take possession of an archive that does not want you, learn the four verbs of the building (the slip, the tube, the index, the press), and find out why a dead man asked for a stranger. By the end of Act I the player must hold in her hands a document that does not exist in any register in the building.

beats: COLD OPEN, TUTORIAL AS THESIS. Twenty minutes out of Rossport, spray has got into Wren's satchel and fused two leaves of her own commission — the legal instrument that is her only authority. In the Ardent's cabin she humidifies, separates and blots it with a spatula and a sheet of Gore-Tex, slowly, in four minutes of pure hand-work, and can damage it permanently by hurrying. No plot lands until she has done it. The game's entire grammar — patience, tools, paper as a physical body — is taught before a single character speaks.

09:40, 26 October. She signs the visitors' book at the wicket. Ottoline Verge, seventy-two and unpaid and delighted, shows her how a requisition slip works: white top copy to the strongroom by tube, pink carbon into the stub book, and the countersignature box. 'If the Warden's out, her clerk initials it p.p. — per procurationem, on behalf of. We've done it since the Ark.' Two millimetres of pencil, taught as an item of housekeeping, by a woman who has no idea what she has just handed the player.

PIKE'S GRIEVANCE (the plant). Halvard Pike refuses to shake her hand and delivers, unprompted, four minutes of contempt about the state of the registry — ending on docketing. 'One hand in this building endorses a folder the Ministry way: on the outside third, upside down to the tag, so you have to turn the whole file over to read your own file. Whitehall, 1958. Everybody else does it like a Christian.' He also squares a treasury tag for her, tail under, loop left, and calls it 'her people's knot.' No prompt, no highlight, no journal entry beyond what the player writes.

THE DULL LIEN. Wren's first statutory duty is to clear the Authority's schedule of outstanding liabilities. Item 14: 'Superannuation — FERRIER-KYNE, S. — reckonable service claim, £2,140 4s arrears in dispute.' A pension squabble. The player crosses it off in the first hour, as the game intends, and will not look at it again until Act IV, when it becomes the only writing in existence in which Sabine asserts that she was working in this building in 1974.

THE SPECIMEN BUNDLE (the twist, in plain sight, at readable resolution, in the first thirty minutes). Sabine Ferrier-Kyne welcomes Wren with total, unhurried courtesy, gives her a key to every room, and hands her a demonstration bundle — nine documents from 1974 — 'so you can see our house style before you start dating things at me.' Every one is signed A. FERRIER. Every one carries, in 2H pencil in the bottom left corner, the notation p.p. The player can zoom to full resolution. The player will pass these documents, or documents exactly like them, forty times.

THE CORONER'S FILE. In the reading room, the inquest papers on Cormac Sallow, seventy-nine, retired Lamp Superintendent, dead 14 September of a fall from the Muniment gallery. Inside: the Authority's own accident report, typed at 16:50 that day, docketed the Ministry way, upside down to the tag — and signed, in a firm upright hand, Sabine Ferrier-Kyne. And Sallow's letter of 11 September, forwarded twice, asking that 'series 14/B be read by a stranger before it leaves this building.'

THE TYPEWRITER SURVEY (skill 2, taught). Standard conservation practice: before appraisal, characterise the office machines. Wren types a specimen sheet on each of the four survivors and mounts them in her casebook. Imperial 66 (Warden's Office, 1961): lower-case a filling with a hard plug of ink and wax, comma printing 0.4mm high, broken descender on y. Underwood 5 (Rolls Room, 1928): lower-case e riding 0.3mm above the baseline, a wandering 3. Olivetti Lettera 32 (Registry, 1966): grey doubling from a slack ribbon vibrator, chipped l. Remington Noiseless (Accounts, 1938): a heavy g from a bent typebar, capitals dropping 0.2mm.

THE MACHINE THAT CANNOT LIE (skill 4, taught). In the Post Room Wren opens the Pitney Postmaster franking meter under her warrant — a GPO offence for anyone else — winds the register drum, reads the descending credit and the ascending total, and reconciles the day's post book against them. A five-minute lesson in serial records, on a machine nobody in 187 years has thought of as a witness.

01:20, 27 October. Rain on glass. Somebody is burning paper in the courtyard incinerator. The scaffolders removed the chimney damper on 2 September (Sandbach's site diary, item 41) so the flue will not draw; the rain comes in through the open head and puts the fire out badly. By the time Wren gets down in her coat over her nightdress the courtyard is empty and the ash grate is a sodden black brick. She rakes it, floats the fragments off in a tray of cold water, and carries them up to the Binding Room to dry between blotters.

She telephones Phyllida Halkett from the Rossport call box on the causeway at low water. Halkett explains, in exhausting detail, the procedure for certifying a series under section 41, and refuses — flatly, three times, and every time she is ever called — to have an opinion about anything that has happened in the building.
acts.gate: Certify three series (1/A Charter and Board Minutes, 2/C Pilotage Licences, 9/E Wreck Register) by completing three escalating appraisal exercises; then stabilise and read the incinerator fragments using the humidification technique taught in the cold open. Cross-check the recovered document against the Register of Notices Issued 1974 in the Long Registry.
acts.cliffhanger: The scorched carbon is a Notice to Mariners, numbered 74/119, drafted 15 August 1974: MARINERS ARE ADVISED THAT THE LIGHT EXHIBITED FROM THE NINE BELLS BEACON MAY NOT BE RELIED UPON UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE. The Register of Notices Issued for 1974 runs 74/118, 74/120. No cancellation, no minute, no gap explained. Somebody wrote the warning. Somebody stopped it. And somebody, in the rain, at twenty past one this morning, was still trying to burn it.

acts.title: SERIES 14/B
acts.goal: Prove that the 1974 Nine Bells file was gutted and retyped, derive exactly what is missing, and get inside the strongroom to look for it. Escalation: from 'a document is odd' to 'seven documents have been removed by name, and the index that betrays them was retyped by a specific machine in a specific year.'
opens: The Muniment Room and Gallery (the rail, the north bay, the map presses, the spectacles)
The Strongroom (Chubb three-movement timelock, series 14/B, the bottom shelf)
The Undercroft (bare bulb, sump, the blind north wall)
The Switchboard Room (twelve-line plug board, call-log books 1946–1991)
The Chart Loft (light table, dividers, the survey drawer)
The Lamp Room (Rita's kingdom; dismounted optics, Sandbach's crate, the Lamp Superintendents' frame)
The Ardent at sea (aborted crossing, four hundred yards off the reef)
Rossport Quay ferry office (booking book, manifest)
The Site Hut and scaffold decks (Sandbach's programme, the strip-out schedule)
beats: THE CARD INDEX GAP. Sixty thousand cards in four hundred drawers, and an index more honest than the archive it describes: weeding a file is an afternoon, weeding an index is a fortnight, so nobody did it. Sorting drawers 214–216 by card stock, ribbon colour and typeface, Wren isolates forty-seven cards retyped on a machine with a raised lower-case e — the Underwood 5 in the Rolls Room — on stock not manufactured before 1987. From the surviving accession numbers she derives seven documents that exist as cards and do not exist as paper. This is the shopping list that drives Acts III and IV.

THE REQUISITION SYSTEM BEGINS TO LIE (and the player writes the evidence herself). Slip 2271, series 14/B box 4, Oil and Stores, Nine Bells 1974 — comes back as 14/A box 4, Oil and Stores, Cadran Point. One character. Deniable. Slip 2283, Despatch Book 1970–79 — comes back NOT TRACED, see W/O 89/2. Wren logs both stubs in her casebook, in her own handwriting, out of professional habit, and thinks nothing of it. Standing Order 7, printed on the back of every slip and read by nobody, requires every reader's requisition to pass the Warden's pigeonhole for countersignature.

OTTOLINE STEERS. Over tea from the kettle in drawer 388, with immense gentleness, she mentions that Mr Pike holds keys to everything, that he has always been very close about the Lights series, and that he was here the evening poor Cormac died. Two of those three things are true.

RITA AND THE DEAKIN LETTER. Marguerite Tain, boatwoman, daughter of the pilot the Rossport Report destroyed, produces from the lamp-room file a letter dated 4 March 1975 from a crewman named Deakin: the beacon was dark, they all knew, they were told to say nothing. It appears to end the case in Act II. Wren, being what she is, says she will have to authenticate it before she can cite it, and Rita hates her for it.

THE ABORTED CROSSING (first sea beat; the silhouette arrives in hour two, not hour four). Rita takes her out on the Ardent to look at the rock. Two miles out the swell gets up over the Sowens and Wren, who is genuinely and unglamorously terrified of open water, is sick over the lee rail while the beacon comes and goes behind grey water — a hundred and twelve feet of granite with a black gallery and a dead lantern. Four hundred yards off, through the glasses, the gallery door is standing open. They turn back. The player has now seen the shape the whole game is pointed at, and felt what it will cost to reach it.

SANDBACH ACCELERATES. The strip-out programme moves forward: the Chart Loft is struck on the 30th, the Rolls Room card index is skipped on the 31st. The schedule is pinned in the site hut and the player can read it. Rooms will start becoming physically unavailable. The building's second state begins — dust sheets off, scaffold in, half the shelving boxed and stencilled LOT 4.

THE TIMELOCK (set-piece). The strongroom door has three winding movements and no keyhole: the movements must be set to the building's own historic closing hours, drawn from the Warden's Order Book, which has recorded the closing hour of every working day since 1946 — and 1974 kept different hours from 1998, and Saturdays different again. Wren winds the movements, spins the handle, and goes in.

LOCKED IN (set-piece, body not file). The door swings to behind her at 18:20 and the movements, now running backwards, will not release until 07:00. At 23:40 the undercroft sump backs up in the rain and water comes under the strongroom door to ankle depth in the dark. For forty minutes the player does nothing intellectual at all: she lifts 1974 boxes off the bottom shelf onto the top shelves by feel, choosing which to save first, with a failing torch. Then, through the ventilation trunk, forty feet of galvanised duct that runs up to the Wardens' Hall landing, she hears two women arguing.

THE ARGUMENT. Fragments, distorted, unattributable: '...forty-seven of them, and I did it with my own hands...' '...he was in the chair, he could not hold a pen, you know that better than anybody...' '...you were never even there, that is the whole of it, you were never there...' And then, for a long time, somebody crying. Wren, in the dark, in four inches of water, writes down every word she is sure of and marks the rest 'not certain' — because that is what she is.

AT THE BACK OF THE BOTTOM SHELF, above the waterline by two inches, a japanned deed box stencilled A. FERRIER, WARDEN. Empty, except for a quarter-century of paper dust, a dead moth, and — pressed flat against the bottom by its own weight — a single sheet of blue-black flimsy: page two of a document whose page one is ash in her Binding Room.

In the Muniment gallery, in the north bay behind the map presses, on the reading slope where nobody has any business working: a pair of folded spectacles on an open ledger, exactly where a man set them down when he stood up to talk to somebody. Nobody has touched them in six weeks. Wren does not touch them either. She photographs them and takes a dust sample from the floor, jar 6.
acts.gate: Sort the forty-seven retyped cards by machine and stock, derive the seven missing accession numbers, and enter them in the casebook as a want-list; then open the Chubb timelock by setting all three movements from the correct historical closing schedule.
acts.cliffhanger: Shut in a flooding strongroom until seven in the morning, listening to two women tear each other apart through a ventilation duct, and unable to say for certain which two. In the morning the door opens on Sabine Ferrier-Kyne with a towel, a cup of tea and a written apology for the state of the building, and Wren cannot tell — will not be able to tell for three more days — whether she is being helped or handled.

acts.title: THE FORGERY
acts.goal: Authenticate the one document that would end the case, watch it die under your own hands, lose your legal authority, and find the archive that a thief has been building for forty years. Escalation: the danger stops being institutional and becomes personal — Wren is disarmed, discredited, and made a trespasser in a building she has a warrant for.
opens: The Tide Room (bricked up June 1975; opened with a crowbar in the rain)
Cardew village and the Cardew Post Office
Call Box, Cardew 4471 (forty yards from the door of a dead man)
Pike's Cottage, Cardew (three thousand documents; the kitchen table)
Rita's shed at the slipway (Cormac Sallow's effects, uncleared)
The Rossport police station (DS Marren Iveson)
Brannock House (the Warden's residence; Absalom Ferrier's sickroom, now a paint store)
beats: THE FIVE-STEP AUTHENTICATION (skill 1, tested; the red herring is the tutorial for the proof). Raking light for the watermark. A chain-line count against the beta-radiograph reference sheets. A fibre loupe at forty power. The postmark gazetteer. A ribbon-ink comparison against the four office specimens. The Deakin letter passes three tests and fails two: the sheet is Ardwell Bond, a stock not manufactured before June 1981, and the franking is Cardew sorting office, which stamped its last item on 30 September 1972. A third tell, which the player may or may not find: the ribbon is nylon, and nylon was not sold for an Adler Gabriele until 1979, and there is an Adler Gabriele in Rita's locker in the Lamp Room.

THE HONEST WITNESS (act turn, promoted from a puzzle to a reversal). Norah Feaver, a passenger, aged nineteen in 1974, told the Rossport Inquiry: 'We could see the light perfectly well. Three flashes. We all saw it.' She was telling the truth, and her truth is the single strongest evidence that the beacon was burning, and it has stood for twenty-four years. In the Chart Loft, with the Admiralty List of Lights for 1974 and a chart of Ivory Sound, Wren establishes that the Nine Bells shows Fl(3) W 20s and the Cadran Point light, nine miles south-south-east, shows Fl(3) W 15s. Three flashes either way. Nobody at the inquiry ever asked a frightened girl to count the seconds. Wren telephones her, in Wolverhampton, from the Rossport call box, and asks her to count them now, on a kitchen clock, from memory. She can.

THE CHART LOFT OVERLAYS, AND THE ROOM THAT WAS NOT THERE (the world doubles). Three transparent surveys of the headland and the approach — 1948, the 1974 buoyage revision, 1998 — registered on the light table by their triangulation marks. Two things fall out. First: the Rossport Inquiry drew the Pelagia's reconstructed track on the 1948 sheet, and against 1974 buoyage she is not where the finding says she was; she is precisely on the line a competent pilot would steer. Second, and nobody was looking for it: the 1948 sheet shows a chamber under the north end of the undercroft that appears on no plan after 1975.

THE CROWBAR IN THE RAIN (set-piece). The undercroft's blind north wall is nine courses of brick in a Portland stone opening, laid in cement that is twenty-three years younger than the wall around it. Works Order 75/188, June 1975, 'seal chamber, damp' — initialled p.p. Wren takes a crowbar off Sandbach's scaffold deck and opens it herself, at night, in horizontal rain, with the site floodlights throwing her shadow forty feet up the granite.

THE TIDE ROOM (the dumb witness). A Kelvin and White stilling-well marigraph, installed 1908, a pen on a clockwork drum, scratching the height of the sea onto smoked paper for sixty-seven years without an opinion in its head. Wren re-inks it, re-hangs the driving weight, winds it, and it starts writing again in front of her. Stacked on the shelf behind it: every drum from 1908 to 1975, including 1974/44. And on a bench, in a bundle tied with tape and never accessioned: the Rossport Inquiry's own working papers, returned to the Authority in 1975 and walled in the same month.

THE LIST OF PERSONS CONSIDERED AND NOT CALLED. Forty-one names, typed on the Underwood 5. Number 29: 'Mrs O. Verge — wife of relief keeper — no direct knowledge — not called', with a small tick in the margin in a hand the player has watched make ticks for three acts. Number 33: 'Miss S. Ferrier — the Warden's private secretary — no official capacity — not called.' The erasure, in ink, in the assessor's own file. Wren does not yet know what it means. She copies it out anyway, because that is the job.

ENID AT THE INCINERATOR. 22:50, 30 October. Enid Charnock, sixty-three, in a coat over her nightdress, feeding the 1974 cash book into a fire that will not take. She surrenders it, weeping, and says one true sentence — 'I only ever did what I was told, and I have the paper to prove it, and that is the worst part' — and then refuses to say another word for two days.

SANDBACH AT TWO IN THE MORNING. The Lamp Room, a hooded torch, a crowbar and a packing crate: two Fresnel panels, the Ardent's binnacle and a hundred and forty kilos of dismounted brass, addressed to a dealer in Antwerp. He gives a panicky, obviously false account of 'salvage recording' and the player is certain, for eighteen hours, that she has found her man in the right room on the right night. He is stealing brass. He is guilty of exactly what he appears guilty of, at about thirty thousand pounds, and of nothing else in this building whatsoever.

THE COLLAPSE. Wren files an honest adverse report on the Deakin letter, because the commission obliges her to, and because she is who she is. Sabine, who is also who she is, reports it to the police the same afternoon at four o'clock with genuine regret and a covering letter offering every assistance. DS Iveson arrests Rita Tain at 17:15 on 31 October. Because the letter was the only evidence that the light was dark, the police shut the whole proposition down with it; the Ministry, informed by fax of a forgery in a series under appraisal, revokes Wren's commission at 16:20 the following afternoon and the fax is timed and filed and the player can read it. Wren has thirty-one hours in which she is a nineteen-year-old girl with no authority standing in somebody else's building.

PIKE, OF ALL PEOPLE. He does not apologise and does not soften. He says: 'The strongroom key is on the third hook and I am going to my dinner,' and leaves. Then, at low water, he drives her over the causeway to Cardew in a Bedford van full of empty boxes, and shows her a rented cottage with three thousand documents in it, catalogued in his own hand on the backs of tide-table covers, removed over forty years to save them from a Ministry circular that ordered them destroyed. He will be prosecuted for it. He knows. He shows her anyway, because she is the only person who has ever asked him what was in them.
acts.gate: Complete all five authentication steps on the Deakin letter and file a truthful adverse report — the game requires the player to destroy her own case with her own hands, and quietly records whether she fudged a step. Then register the three chart overlays to reveal the sealed chamber, and open it.
acts.cliffhanger: On Pike's kitchen table, under a bare bulb, three books: the Light Dues Ledger, the Oil Requisition Book for the Nine Bells 1966–1980, and the Keeper's Wage Sheets. Week by week, from 1 July to 31 December 1974, the player fills in a Conservancy reconciliation form. Dues are collected every week. Wages are paid every week. Oil stops on Saturday 24 August 1974 and never resumes: seventy-one days, ten complete dues weeks, one thousand one hundred and eighty-two ships charged four thousand one hundred and eighty pounds four shillings for a light that was not burning. There is no hint, no highlight and no chime. The third column simply refuses to agree, and the music stops. Three requisitions — R.741, R.748, R.755 — are stamped REQUISITION NOT SANCTIONED — REFER WINTER REFIT, over the initials of a hand Wren cannot read, and the notation p.p.

acts.title: PER PROCURATIONEM
acts.goal: Give the hand a name, and get the last document off the rock. Escalation: from an institution's crime to a woman's; the archive begins to burn, the telephone line goes down, the causeway closes, and the sea is the only way left to the evidence.
opens: The Nine Bells Beacon: Landing Stage and Doorway
The Nine Bells Beacon: Oil Store (cold paraffin, the keeper's log)
The Nine Bells Beacon: Service Room (the stove, the bunk, the long night)
The Nine Bells Beacon: Lantern Room and Gallery (the clockwork optic, the brass sector plates)
The Roof and Signal Mast, Pilotage House
Ottoline's cottage, 4 Coastguard Row
The Stationery Store (Enid's return-before-issue shelf)
Pike's Cottage, burning, and after
beats: PER PROCURATIONEM (the twist puzzle). A light table, a magnifier, and forty-eight documents from 1974, all signed A. FERRIER, all recovered from four separate sources so that no single custodian could have faked the set. The player is asked to sort them into two piles: signed, and signed per procurationem. Seven fall out clean — genuine, shaky, unmistakably a man's hand, dated 2–10 August and 18 November onwards. The other forty-one, every document from 11 August to 3 November 1974, are p.p. There is no second pile. The signature is not forged. It is scrupulously, legally honest. It is a woman signing on behalf of a man who could not hold a pen, exactly as Standing Order 4 permitted, and no law anywhere required anybody to write down who she was.

THE PROOF OF INCAPACITY (three independent sources, because one is a claim and three are a fact). Dr Munn's locum mileage claims: Brannock House, fourteen miles, twice weekly, from 12 August. Nurse Kilbride's visit ledger, found in a paint store that used to be a sickroom: 'pt. hemiplegic R side, no speech, cannot hold pen, wife present.' And the Warden's Order Book, whose leaves for 11 August to 3 November were taken out at the gutter with a razor in 1989 — and whose facing pages still carry the mirror-image offset of the ink that pressed against them for fifteen years. Wren reads a razored-out order backwards in a shaving mirror under raking light, and it is the deferment of the relief keeper.

OTTOLINE BREAKS. Wren does not accuse her. She lays out, in order and without comment: the forty-seven cards, the card stock date, the Underwood's raised e, the wage sheets with 'at station' struck through, and the Inquiry's rejected-witness list with a tick beside number 29 in Ottoline's own hand. Ottoline made very sure it stayed easy for them not to call her. She goes home and comes back with a biscuit tin: Cass Verge's letter of 18 August 1974 — residence deferred, wages to continue, you will not discuss this — initialled p.p. She has kept it for twenty-four years believing she was protecting Absalom Ferrier, and she says, without self-pity, 'I let a whole town blame a dead man to keep them from thinking about mine. I knew it every day. I made the tea and I knew it every day.'

THE MONDAY FERRY. Enid Charnock resigns and takes the 08:15 out with the 1974 cash book in her shopping bag. Rita — on police bail, forbidden to enter Pilotage House, and therefore the only person free to be useful — runs her down on Rossport quay and does not argue with her, just sits with her for an hour. Enid unfolds the back cover: a memorandum from the Warden's Office to the Cashier, dated 6 November 1974, three days after the wreck. 'The Nine Bells oil column is to be carried to Sundry Adjustments (Lights) pending refit.' Initialled p.p. She has looked at it perhaps four hundred times in ninety-six quarters and never once let it mean what it means.

THE SWITCHBOARD (machine, not paper). A twelve-line plug board, the night-duty roster and the call-log book for 3 November 1974. Re-patching the board reconstructs the hour: 23:06 the coastguard relay, 23:11 the harbourmaster, 23:19 Rossport. And, twenty-three minutes before impact, an outgoing at 22:41 from extension 2 — the Warden's Office, on a Sunday night — to Cardew 4471, four minutes, no answer recorded. The 1974 directory lists Cardew 4471 as the public call box outside Cardew Post Office: forty yards from the front door of the relief keeper who should have been on that rock. Somebody in an empty office rang a man who was in the Ship Inn, and let it ring for four minutes, twenty-three minutes too late.

THE OUTSIDE WITNESS. The plug-log is the Authority's own book and the Board will say so. The GPO's itemised trunk account for Q4 1974, in Enid's ledgers, is not: 3.11.74, Cardew, 22.41, 4 min, 1s 9d, initialled EC. A record kept by strangers, for money, about which nobody in this building had a vote.

THE FOUR REFUSALS (the forged tide board, paid off). Wren lays out her own nine days of requisition stubs — every one in her handwriting, logged out of habit since Act I. Four came back wrong. Every one passed the Warden's pigeonhole under Standing Order 7 and carries her countersignature. Sabine never refused Wren anything; she granted her everything, and steered four things, and the shape of what was steered is the shape of the crime. The evidence of the surveillance is in the victim's own hand, and has been since the first morning.

THE 'a' CURVE (skill 2, escalated). The Imperial 66's lower-case a has been filling with ink and wax since 1961 at a rate the player can now plot from dated specimens. The 1974 refusals sit on the curve at partial occlusion. The 1998 accident report sits at full. The relabelled box 17 sits at full. Same machine, same room, twenty-four years apart, and the machine will say so under oath.

THE RIBBON (institutional pettiness as the preserver of truth). Enid's stationery rule since 1968: no new ribbon issued until the used spool is returned. The Imperial 66's September 1998 spool is on the shelf in the Stationery Store with a docket on it. Read backwards under magnification, the last two hundred characters run, in unbroken sequence: 12.9.98 — 'I know what you mean to send. Please do not send it. There is nothing in it that can help anybody now. S.' — a letter typed and never sent — and then, immediately after it on the same ribbon, with no ribbon change between, the accident report of 14 September. She knew what he intended, two days before he died, and she has said in writing three times that she did not.

THE OBJECTS THAT CANNOT BE EXPLAINED BY HER OFFICE. Sandbach's site diary, the one contemporaneous daily record in the building that Sabine does not control: 2 September, 'gallery rail nth bay, baluster 3 loose, made safe pending order.' 15 September, 'gallery rail nth bay made good at Warden's personal instruction, out of programme, no order no., not billed.' The morning after a man went over that rail, it was quietly repaired off the books. The Fuel and Light Book: the gallery time-switch, twenty minutes a winding, wound eleven times on 14 September — two hundred and twenty minutes of light for an eighty-eight-minute visit. The Duplicating Book: the Reprax counter jumped forty-one that day against twelve logged. And in the Warden's own Board of Dissolution working file, correctly foliated, correctly indexed, docketed the Ministry way: twenty-six Reprax copies of the contents of series 14/B box 17, four of which are copies of documents that are no longer in box 17. She copied the evidence, destroyed the originals, and filed the copies, because she is an archivist and destruction is the one thing she has never in her life been able to make herself do.

THE FIRE (set-piece, body not file). 22:40, 1 November. Pike's cottage at Cardew goes up — a paraffin heater, a sixty-six-year-old man asleep in a chair, and three thousand documents. Wren gets him out through the scullery window and then goes back in twice. The player chooses, in smoke, with a wet towel over her face, which four of nine bundles to carry out, and lives with it: the ones she leaves are gone from the game and gone from the Board.

CUT OFF. The gale takes the telephone pole at the Cardew turn. No line to Rossport, no ferry until the storm drops, the causeway under six feet of water. Wren climbs to the roof of Pilotage House in horizontal rain, finds the Aldis lamp under a tarpaulin, looks up the international code in the Signal Book because she does not know it, and signals across four miles of black water until Rossport signal station answers.

THE CROSSING (the big one). Dawn, 2 November, rising gale. The refused requisitions are worthless unless she can authenticate them against something the Authority never held — and the Nine Bells keeper's log has been sealed in the beacon's oil store since 1974. Rita, on bail, takes her out in the Ardent because nobody else can handle the boat. Wren is sick twice, hands white on the rail, and jumps for the landing on the rise. Inside: the oil store, and the smell of cold paraffin that has not moved in twenty-four years. The log, in the rack. Final entry, 24 August 1974, 22.10: 'No. 2 vapor. cracked. Oil out. Light down. Nothing more to be done here.' And on the back of the last page, in pencil, a shopping list — tea, boot polish, a birthday card for Nan.

SABINE IS ON THE STAIR. Not with a weapon. With a satchel, a thermos, and the Kestrel Bequest: a bank mandate and a shell trust deed, established 4 April 1977 out of her mother's legacy, thirty-one index-linked standing orders paid monthly for twenty-one years from an account no auditor ever queried because the amounts were too small to be interesting. The player matches beneficiary initials against the Pelagia manifest. Thirty of them are the dependants of the drowned. The thirty-first is M. TAIN — paid, every month since 1977, to the daughter of the man the Authority destroyed, who has spent twenty-four years and every penny of it trying to prove the Authority destroyed him.
acts.gate: Complete the p.p. sort (identify the boundary dates 11 August and 18 November 1974 unaided) and cite three independent proofs of Absalom Ferrier's incapacity; recover the Nine Bells keeper's log from the oil store; recover at least four of the nine bundles from the fire.
acts.cliffhanger: The sea gets up past the point where the Ardent can lie off the landing. Rita runs for Cardew with the log in a dry bag and the two women are left on the rock: a fifty-eight-year-old Warden and a nineteen-year-old apprentice, alone in a beacon for eleven hours with a paraffin stove and everything each of them knows. At about two in the morning Sabine says: 'Ask me. You have all of it now, or near enough. Ask me and I will tell you the truth, and then in the morning you will have to decide what to do with it, and I promise you that is the harder half.'

acts.title: THE NINE BELLS
acts.goal: Turn twenty-four years of paper into a case that survives challenge, argue it in front of a Board that will strike anything you cannot cite, refer a homicide you can prove but not feel certain about, and put the light back on. Confrontation and resolution.
opens: The Nine Bells Service Room, 02:00–07:00 (the confession that is worth nothing)
The Nine Bells Lantern Room by night (the optic, the sector plates, the falling weight)
The Board Room, Pilotage House (the only fully sunlit background in the game)
The Rossport police station, interview room 2 (DS Iveson and the referral form)
St Bride's churchyard, evening (thirty-one slate markers, and one more name read out)
beats: THE CONFESSION THAT IS WORTH NOTHING. In the service room, by the stove, Sabine tells her all of it, plainly, without excuse and without much emotion, over four hours. And the game then does the hardest and best thing it can do: at dawn, DS Iveson tells Wren over the radio that a confession made to one nineteen-year-old girl on a rock in a gale, unrecorded, uncautioned and uncorroborated, is worth precisely nothing, and that she should stop crying about it and go and do her job. Everything must still be cited. Nothing the player has been told may be used. Only what she can hold up to a window.

FIRST LIGHT, 3 NOVEMBER 1998, the anniversary. Before she goes down to the boat, Wren does the one thing in the game that is not evidence. The clockwork optic has been dead since 1974 and it is incomplete — two Fresnel panels went to Antwerp in Ivo Sandbach's crate. He gives one back. He drives to Rossport at four in the morning to buy it off a shipping agent with money he does not have, and hands it to her wrapped in a fleece, and says nothing about his daughters or his firm or the fourteen thousand pounds, and this is the only decent thing he does in the game and it is enough. Wren sets the brass occulting sector plates on the rotation drum, winds the weight, and sets the escapement release for 23:04. Three flashes. Twenty seconds. The true character of the Nine Bells, entered by hand, as a physical input, by a girl who worked it out from an Admiralty list and a frightened woman counting on a kitchen clock. The moral fact of the case, set into a machine.

ASSEMBLING THE FILE. A table, nine core exhibits, forty-one supporting documents, and a Conservancy case file with a citation column that cannot be left blank. The player builds eight links — presence, means, opportunity, signature, identity, motive, consciousness of guilt, historical predicate — and every assertion must be tied to a document by accession number. The casebook has been doing this since Act I; now it is scored.

THE BOARD OF DISSOLUTION, 14:00. Chairman Mrs Ellary Voss (Lord Chancellor's nominee), assessor Captain Dunnet, and Mr Pargeter for the Ministry, whose job is to strike. Named counter-evidence is fired at every weak link: the 1975 finding and its statutory presumption of correctness; the Deakin forgery, offered as proof that this whole line of enquiry is a fantasy already once faked; Pike's forty years of theft, offered as a chain-of-custody attack on half the exhibits; Rita Tain's arrest; and, at the last, Sabine's counsel asking on what evidence a Board proposes to name a person whom no record of this Authority has ever named. Wren answers that one with the Authority's own pension file, item 14 of the liabilities schedule, in which Sabine Ferrier-Kyne asserts under her own signature that she was employed here in 1974 — the only document in 187 years in which she asked to be counted.

THE STRIKING. Any assertion the player cannot cite is struck, aloud, in front of her, and the transcript prints with the gaps in it. This is not a fail state; it is a score, and the score is the ending. The player is watching, in real time, a mechanised proof of whether the game played fair and whether she did the work.

THE REFERRAL. Separately, in interview room 2 at Rossport, Wren makes a homicide referral on the death of Cormac Sallow, and the game requires her to word it herself from a menu of what she can actually prove. The physical evidence supports a grab and a fall from a rail known to be defective, not a push; the seventeen minutes before the 999 call, the off-programme repair, the twenty-nine Reprax impressions and the ribbon support everything after. Wren can write 'murder' and watch it fall apart, or write what the paper says and watch it stand. Iveson tells her, not unkindly, that the second one is the one that puts people in prison.

23:04. From the Board Room window, from the churchyard, from the quay at Rossport, from Cardew, from the ferry: nine miles out in the dark, the Nine Bells shows three flashes in twenty seconds for the first time since Saturday 24 August 1974. Nobody has to explain it to anybody on that coast. Rita Tain, on bail, standing at the slipway, sits down on the wet concrete.

NOTICE TO MARINERS 74/119. In every ending, without exception, the notice is issued: retyped from the scorched carbon on the Imperial 66, run off on the Reprax, franked with a single fourpenny impression struck from the old die under the meter's descending register, entered in the Register of Notices Issued in the correct place with the correct date and a note of the delay, and posted to all two hundred and fourteen addressees on Schedule D — beginning, as statutory precedence requires, with No. 1, the Keeper, Nine Bells Beacon. Twenty-four years, two months and eighteen days late. Appended to it, at Wren's own insistence and against Conservancy house style, are thirty-one names.
acts.gate: Survive the Board: every assertion in the case file must carry a citation to a document the player physically holds, and each of the eight links must survive its named counter-evidence. The finding, the exoneration and the referral are all direct functions of how many links stand.
acts.cliffhanger: There is no cliffhanger, only a last unscored choice, which the game does not grade and does not comment on. Wren knows where Rita Tain's thirty-four pounds a month has come from since 1977. Nobody else living knows, the trust deed does not name the settlor, and the Board does not need it. On the quay, with the ferry loading, Rita asks her straight out whether there is anything else. The player answers, and the game ends on Rita's face, and then on the light.

cast.name: Sabine Ferrier-Kyne
cast.role: Warden of the Brannock Pilotage Authority (appointed 1991), presiding over its dissolution. Daughter of Warden Absalom Ferrier (1911–1979). Unpaid private secretary to her father 1959–1976; Clerk Grade III from 1976; Deputy Warden 1984. A fortnight from appointment to the National Maritime Heritage Board — the first title she will ever have held in her own name. THE CULPRIT.
cast.appearance: Tall and narrow and upright as a plumb line, five foot ten, no stoop at all at fifty-eight. Iron-grey hair cut short and set once a fortnight, combed straight back off a high bony forehead. A long face; deep vertical folds from nose to mouth; pale grey eyes with slightly slack lower lids; a wide thin mouth. Big-knuckled hands, nails cut square and short, no varnish, a thin gold wedding band worn on the right hand since she was widowed in 1991. Wears three things in rotation: a charcoal wool skirt suit with a faintly military shoulder, a cream blouse with a small round collar, and a cardigan the colour of wet slate kept over the shoulders indoors like a stole. A 2H pencil behind the right ear at all times, sharpened with a blade, never a sharpener. Reading glasses on a black cord. CHARACTERISTIC EXPRESSION: a small, entirely genuine, entirely attentive smile that arrives about half a second late, as though she had to finish a sentence in her head first.
cast.personality: The most competent person in any room she has ever been in, and the only one who has never once said so. Courteous to the point of being unanswerable. Answers questions completely, which is a kind of armour. Tidies as she talks — squares a stack of paper, moves a cup onto a coaster, closes a drawer with two fingers. Has an archivist's incapacity for destruction and a bureaucrat's incapacity for improvisation, and the whole catastrophe of her life is the one afternoon she had to improvise. Genuinely likes Wren, and says so, and means it, and it is the most dangerous thing in the building.
cast.speechStyle: Complete sentences with the subordinate clauses in the right places. Uses the passive voice for anything she did and the active for anything anyone else did, unconsciously and constantly — 'the requisition was refused', 'Mr Pike removed the boxes' — and a player who notices this in Act I has the whole game. Gives dates without hesitating. Never says 'I think'; says 'the position is'. Calls Wren 'Miss Adare' for four days and 'Wren' exactly once, on the rock.
cast.motive: Two things she cannot survive losing: her father's name and, at last, her own. The Heritage Board appointment is a fortnight away after thirty-nine years of doing the work under somebody else's signature. Beneath that is the older and unspeakable one: she is the only person alive who knows that the Authority's crime was not committed by 'the Authority'.
cast.secret: Between 11 August and 18 November 1974 she was the Brannock Pilotage Authority. Her father had a cerebral haemorrhage on Sunday 11 August; she found him. The Authority was four months from insolvency, the bank had refused further facility on 15 August, and the Ministry's quinquennial review was sitting: an authority discovered to be rudderless would have been abolished, its sixty staff dismissed and its 163 years of records dispersed. So she ran it, and signed everything p.p. A. Ferrier, because Article 9 of the Charter of 1811 required the Warden to be 'a man of full age'. She deferred the relief keeper on 18 August with wages continuing, refused three oil requisitions to the winter refit, struck Notice to Mariners 74/119 from the despatch docket on 16 August, and went on collecting light dues because stopping them would have raised a question in Accounts. The beacon went dark at 21:10 on Saturday 24 August. At 22:34 on Sunday 3 November the Rossport coastguard telephoned to ask whether the Nine Bells was exhibiting; at 22:41 she rang the call box at Cardew and let it ring for four minutes at a man who was in the pub; at 23:04 the Pelagia struck. Because officially she had never been there, the Rossport Inquiry did not call her, question her, or list her among those present. Since 4 April 1977 she has paid thirty-one anonymous index-linked annuities out of her mother's legacy through a trust called the Kestrel Bequest. On Monday 14 September 1998 she went up to the Muniment gallery to persuade Cormac Sallow not to send his letter; he refused; she took the folder; he went over a rail she knew was loose. She stood there for eleven minutes, then went down, rang Rossport, photocopied twenty-six sheets, reshelved the box, typed the accident report at ten to five and signed it in her own name for the first time in her life.
cast.alibi: For 14 September 1998: 'I was in the Board Room the whole of that morning with the quantity surveyor; I did not know Mr Sallow was in the building until Mrs Verge came running.' For 1974: 'My father ran this Authority until his retirement in 1976. I typed for him.' Both are documents-deep and both fail to documents.
lies: 'I never saw Mr Sallow that morning — I was in the Board Room with the quantity surveyor.' CAUGHT IN ACT IV: requisition slip R98/2211 is initialled in the 'issued by' column by the Warden, because Pike was on the 08:15 ferry (Rossport ferry booking book); and Sandbach's site diary puts the quantity surveyor's meeting on the 15th, not the 14th.

'Series 14/B was reboxed in 1989 because of mould. Nothing was withdrawn.' CAUGHT IN ACT II: forty-seven index cards retyped on 1987 stock, seven accession numbers with cards and no documents, and the reboxing schedule attached to her own memorandum W/O 89/2 listing twenty-three items in box 17 against seventeen present.

'My father ran this Authority until 1976. I typed for him.' CAUGHT IN ACT IV: the p.p. sort, Dr Munn's mileage claims, Nurse Kilbride's ledger, and the mirror offsets of the razored Order Book leaves.

'I have no interest in the outcome. I am a fortnight from an appointment and I would frankly rather be finished with all of it.' CAUGHT IN ACT IV by something the player themselves dismissed in Act I: item 14 of the liabilities schedule, her superannuation claim, in which she asserts under her own signature that her reckonable service runs from 1959.

'You have had every box in this building that you have asked for.' CAUGHT IN ACT IV: her own countersignature, under Standing Order 7, on the four requisition slips of the nine that came back substituted or not traced. The player's own handwriting is the exhibit.

'I had no idea what Mr Sallow intended to send to your people.' CAUGHT IN ACT IV: the used ribbon spool from the Imperial 66, on which the sentence 'I know what you mean to send. Please do not send it.' sits two days above the accident report with no ribbon change between them.

'I did not push him.' NEVER DISPROVED, AND TRUE. The game gives the player no evidence of a push and considerable evidence of a grab and a defective rail, and requires her to word the referral accordingly. It is the only completely honest thing Sabine says in nine days and the player will not believe it.
cast.arc: From the most helpful person in the building to the only person in it, and the reframe is total and contradicts nothing. Her courtesy was never obstruction; she opened every door because she had already read every box, and the only series she could not control was the one Pike had stolen before she got to it. Her 1989 memorandum, signed openly in her own name, is not the cover-up — it is a woman with real authority at last, tidying up after the ghost she used to be. Her fight against Rita's campaign was never institutional loyalty: clearing Emrys Tain requires somebody to ask who else could have signed. On the rock she is neither monster nor martyr; she is a woman who was refused a name, used the refusal to escape, has paid thirty-one people every month for twenty-one years, and killed a man to keep a fortnight-old appointment. Depending on the player's file she is arrested on the Board Room steps, arrested at Rossport for the 1974 offences only, or walks out to the harbour with her satchel and is not seen again, and the last shot of that ending is the light coming on behind her.

cast.name: Halvard Pike
cast.role: Chief Clerk. Copy boy 1954, aged twenty-two; forty-four years in the building. Runs the registry, the pneumatic tube system and the requisition slips, and regards the archive as his own body. The most obvious suspect in the game for three full acts.
cast.appearance: Short and heavy through the chest, five foot six, stooped from forty years of hauling boxes off high shelves. Bald across the crown with grey hair combed flat across it and grey hair in the ears. A bulbous, broken-veined nose; small wet blue eyes; a permanent shaving cut on the left jaw. Brown cotton warehouse coat over a shirt and a knitted maroon tie, sleeve garters above the elbow, cuffs gone shiny. Thick-lensed National Health spectacles mended at the left hinge with copper wire. Ineradicable purple ink on the first two fingers of the right hand and a nail on the right thumb split by a box lid in 1979. CHARACTERISTIC EXPRESSION: chin tucked, looking at you over the top of the glasses with contemptuous patience, as though waiting for you to finish being young.
cast.personality: Rude on principle and correct on detail. Believes, accurately, that the Conservancy will microfilm the interesting ten per cent and pulp the rest, and cannot forgive Wren for being its instrument. Physically incapable of watching somebody mishandle a book. Grieving, though he would rather die than call it that: dissolution deletes him, and he has no wife, no hobby and no house that is not full of other people's paper.
cast.speechStyle: Short, flat, declarative, with the local vowels. Uses shelf-marks as nouns in ordinary conversation. Says 'that's not a document, that's a photocopy' as an insult. Never finishes a sentence about himself. In Act III, at his kitchen table, talks for eleven minutes without stopping and cannot look at her while he does it.
cast.motive: Not to protect a crime — to protect a filing system he believes is the only true record of a coast, from a dissolution he cannot stop. He is right about the pulping, which is what makes him unbearable.
cast.secret: He has removed roughly three thousand documents over forty years to a rented cottage at Cardew, catalogued in his own hand on the backs of tide-table covers. It is theft under the Coastal Services Act and he will be prosecuted for it. He did it because in 1985 Ministry Circular 12/85 ordered the Lights records destroyed on transfer of the beacon to Trinity House, so he carried them home in the van instead. He has never once read the Nine Bells material he rescued, because it was filed under Lights and he is a Pilotage man, and that distinction has cost twenty-four years. Everything Sabine weeded from 14/B in 1989, Pike had already quietly taken in 1985 — and neither of them knew.
cast.alibi: For 14 September 1998: 'I was here all evening.' He was not; he was at Cardew unloading a crate of stolen documents and would rather be a murder suspect than say so.
lies: 'Nothing has ever left this building on my watch.' CAUGHT IN ACT III when he shows her the cottage himself; the earlier tell is in Act II, where the discharge stamps in the accession registers for the Lights series are in his hand and go nowhere.
'I've no notion where the Despatch Books went. Ask the Warden, she reboxed everything.' CAUGHT IN ACT III: Despatch Book 1970–79 is on his kitchen dresser.

'I was here all evening on the fourteenth of September.' CAUGHT IN ACT IV: the ferry booking book has him back on the headland at 17:40 and the Cardew garage fuel book has him buying four gallons at 18:20 nine miles away.

'I know every document in this building.' The boast, not the fact, and it is the tragedy. CAUGHT IN ACT III when Wren asks him what is in the box marked LIGHTS: STORES 1966–80 and he cannot tell her, because he never opened it.
cast.arc: From the game's loudest suspect to its unlikeliest custodian. His theft is the single reason the evidence still exists. He hands Wren the strongroom key on the day she has no legal right to it, drives her to Cardew in a van full of empty boxes, and nearly dies in the fire because he went back for a bundle. In the strongest ending the Board records that the Nine Bells finding could not have been made without documents unlawfully removed by the Chief Clerk, and recommends that no penalty be imposed; he is convicted anyway, fined two hundred pounds, and dies in 2004 having spent his last five years as an unpaid volunteer at the Conservancy's Ilberry store, where they let him keep a warehouse coat on a hook with his name on it.

cast.name: Marguerite "Rita" Tain
cast.role: Lamp-room curator and boatwoman. Runs the pilot cutter Ardent and the crossing to the Nine Bells. Employed by the Authority she has been publicly accusing since 1976, because nobody else on the coast can handle the boat. Daughter of Emrys Tain, the pilot who went down with the Pelagia and was posthumously blamed for her.
cast.appearance: Wiry and weathered, five foot four, forearms and hands like a boatwoman's, knuckles thickened. Dark hair going iron at the temples, cut short by herself with kitchen scissors and never quite level. Broad flat face, high colour across the cheekbones, a white scar through the left eyebrow from a davit in 1988. Navy fisherman's smock over a fleece, black oilskin trousers, sea boots turned down at the top, a brass whistle on a green lanyard. Nicotine on the first two fingers, a roll-up behind the ear in the dry. CHARACTERISTIC EXPRESSION: jaw set, chin slightly up, eyes going past your shoulder to look at the weather.
cast.personality: Twenty-four years of being right and being disbelieved have burned everything soft out of her except a completely unguarded tenderness toward old people and boats. Refused legal aid four times. Currently being sued for defamation by a retired inquiry assessor she named in a pamphlet. Cannot take help without insulting the person offering it. Superb at sea and impossible ashore.
cast.speechStyle: Fast, clipped, profane, full of half-finished sentences she assumes you can complete. Recites the 1975 findings verbatim, with the paragraph numbers, the way other people recite prayers. Goes completely silent when she is frightened, which is how you know.
cast.motive: Her father's name. That is the entire content of her life since she was twenty-five, and she has spent every penny she has ever had on it — including, without knowing it, thirty-four pounds a month from the woman who caused it.
cast.secret: In 1996, out of money and out of options, she wrote the Deakin letter herself and slipped it into the lamp-room file: a fabricated 1975 confession from a crewman stating the beacon was dark. She is ashamed of it in a way she cannot say out loud, and the shame is the reason she is so vicious about everybody else's honesty. She also has, in the shed at the slipway, three cardboard boxes of Cormac Sallow's effects, which she cleared after the funeral and has never opened, because he tried to tell her something in August and she was too angry to listen.
cast.alibi: For 14 September 1998: out at the Nine Bells servicing the fog signal, alone, from 07:30 to 15:00 — true, and confirmed by the fog-signal service book she has just told Wren she does not keep.
lies: 'The Deakin letter came to me anonymously in 1996, in a brown envelope, no covering note.' CAUGHT IN ACT III by paper forensics: Ardwell Bond, unissued before June 1981; the Cardew sorting-office frank, last struck 30 September 1972; and, for the thorough, a nylon ribbon on an Adler Gabriele that stands in her own locker in the Lamp Room.

'I've never had a penny off anybody in my life.' CAUGHT IN ACT V, and she is not lying — she genuinely believes the standing order is a legacy from her father's union. The post office book she shows Wren for an entirely different reason has twenty-one years of it in the paying-in column.
'I cleared Cormac's rooms and there was nothing in them worth keeping.' CAUGHT IN ACT III/IV: three boxes in her shed, unopened, one of them containing his file copy of oil requisition R.755.

'I don't go out to the rock in the off season. Nobody does.' CAUGHT IN ACT II when the beacon's gallery door is standing open at four hundred yards, and in Act III by the fog-signal service book with her initials against every month since 1991.
cast.arc: The most honest red herring in the game: she is right about absolutely everything except the evidence. She forged a document that says exactly what the truth turns out to be, and in doing so nearly destroyed the truth, and the game lets her feel that all the way down. Arrested at 17:15 on 31 October; on bail by 2 November and therefore the only person in the story free to move; takes the boat out into a gale for the girl who broke her; and in the best ending stands on the slipway at 23:04 and watches three flashes in twenty seconds and sits down on the wet concrete. Whether she is ever told where the thirty-four pounds came from is the last, unscored choice the player makes.

cast.name: Ottoline Verge
cast.role: Registrar of the Rolls, retired 1991. Still comes in six days a week, unpaid, to maintain the card index, because nobody else alive understands it. Keeps a kettle, a tin of biscuits and a pair of sheepskin slippers in drawer 388. Widow of Cass Verge, relief keeper of the Nine Bells.
cast.appearance: Small and round-shouldered, five foot nothing in her slippers. Soft white hair in a low bun held with a tortoiseshell comb, wisps escaping at the nape. A face made almost entirely of kind creases; pale blue eyes behind gold half-moon spectacles on a beaded chain; a slight tremor in the left hand she has had since 1989. Lilac twinset, pleated tweed skirt, thick brown tights, a wedding ring worn to a wire. A cardigan permanently over the back of her chair with a folded handkerchief in the pocket and a rubber thimble on the second finger. CHARACTERISTIC EXPRESSION: delighted to see you. Always. Without exception. Including on the morning she is caught.
cast.personality: The warmest person in the building and the most frightening, and the game asks the player to notice that those are not opposites. Immaculate professional memory for accession numbers going back to 1949 and a vagueness about the autumn of 1974 that is not how memory fails. Makes tea for people she is steering. Genuinely loves the index, which is the only thing in her life she has never lied about.
cast.speechStyle: Soft, unhurried, digressive on purpose — she buries the load-bearing sentence in the middle of an anecdote about somebody's wedding. Says 'oh, now' before every evasion, which the player can learn to hear. When she finally tells the truth in Act IV she does it in short flat sentences with no digressions at all, and the change in rhythm is the emotional event.
cast.motive: Her husband's name, and now her grandson's. Cass Verge was on the wage sheet as relief keeper for the autumn of 1974 and never went out to the rock; he took eleven weeks of money for a light he did not tend, drank steadily for seven years and died in 1981 without ever saying why. If the reconciliation is published, the last name in the ledger is his — and Emlyn Verge is in his second year at the naval college at Ilberry.
cast.secret: She has known since 1975 that the beacon was dark; Cass told her once, drunk, and never again. She was not called to the Rossport Inquiry — and she typed the assessor's list of persons considered and not called, and put a small tick beside her own name. Twenty-four years of arranging not to be asked. In 1989, when the reboxing of 14/B gave her the excuse, she retyped forty-seven index cards on the Underwood 5 to break the cross-references that led from the Nine Bells stores file to the relief keeper's wage sheet. She did not know the refusals came from Sabine. She thought she was covering for Absalom Ferrier, and she thought that was loyalty.
cast.alibi: For 14 September 1998: on the wicket all morning, in full view, which is true, and which is exactly why she is the one who saw who went up.
lies: 'Oh, now — I can't recall the autumn of '74 at all, dear. I was in Accounts in those days.' CAUGHT IN ACT II: the staff register puts her in the Registrar's office from 1968 and her initials are on the Rolls returns for every quarter of 1974.

'The cards have never been retyped. Not in my time, and I've been here since the Ark.' CAUGHT IN ACT II: forty-seven cards on stock not manufactured before 1987, typed on a machine with a raised lower-case e that stands four feet from her chair.

'Mr Pike has keys to everything, you know. Everything. And he was here the evening poor Cormac died.' The steer. Two of the three clauses are true and the third is a guess she lets Wren treat as a fact. CAUGHT IN ACT IV by the ferry book and the Cardew fuel book.

'Cass was out on the rock the whole of that autumn. I hardly saw him.' CAUGHT IN ACT IV by the letter in her own biscuit tin, and by the wage sheets on which somebody has struck through 'at station' in eleven consecutive weeks.

'Nobody ever asked me anything, dear. Nobody ever thought to.' CAUGHT IN ACT III: the Rossport Inquiry's list of persons considered and not called, number 29, Mrs O. Verge, typed on her own machine, with a tick beside it in her own hand.
cast.arc: The culprit's crime at reduced scale, which is the whole point of her, and the game makes the mirroring explicit in Act IV. Sabine spent twenty-four years not being named because the institution refused to name her; Ottoline spent twenty-four years not being called because she typed the list herself. Both let a dead man be blamed to protect a name. One of them killed somebody about it and one of them made tea about it, and Wren has to decide whether that is a difference in kind or only in nerve. Ottoline hands over the biscuit tin unprompted, gives a full statement to DS Iveson, is charged with nothing, and is at the Board on 3 November in her best coat. In the strongest ending she asks to be allowed to read the thirty-one names aloud, and the Chairman lets her, and she gets to number fourteen before Wren has to take over.

cast.name: Enid Charnock
cast.role: Cashier and Accountant to the Authority since 1962. Light dues, wage sheets, petty cash, the stationery ledger and the postage register. Signed the quarterly light-dues returns in 1974 as junior cashier, aged thirty-nine.
cast.appearance: Angular and flat-chested, five foot six, always slightly braced. Hair dyed a determined chestnut and set in tight fortnightly curls; a long nose; a lipstick line drawn a little outside the natural lip; bifocals with a gold upper rim; a small gold crucifix. Bottle-green pussy-bow blouse, A-line skirt, low court shoes, a cardigan buttoned to the throat in all weathers. A bunch of eleven small keys on a retractable chain clipped at the waist, and a rubber finger-stall. CHARACTERISTIC EXPRESSION: watchful, apologising in advance, eyes going to the door of the Warden's Office roughly every ninety seconds.
cast.personality: Meticulous, devout, frightened, and possessed of the most valuable habit in the building: she has never thrown anything away that a rule said to keep. Describes her terror of Sabine as respect and has done for thirty-six years. Runs the stationery ledger like a customs post — no new typewriter ribbon issued until the used spool is returned — and that petty economy, more than any act of courage by anyone, is what hangs the case.
cast.speechStyle: Precise about figures and vague about everything else. Answers a question about a person with an answer about a ledger. Prefaces bad news with 'I'm sure there's an explanation.' Under pressure her sentences get shorter and her arithmetic gets faster.
cast.motive: She has been quietly falsifying a reconciliation for ninety-six quarters. In November 1974 she noticed the Nine Bells oil column was empty, raised it once in writing, and was told by the Warden's Office to carry it to sundries pending refit. She did — every quarter, for twenty-four years, in a column she invented for the purpose. Confessing means admitting she was told, in writing, three days after the wreck.
cast.secret: She kept the instruction. The memorandum of 6 November 1974 is folded inside the back cover of the 1974 cash book, where she has looked at it perhaps four hundred times, and it is initialled p.p. — which she has always taken to mean the Warden was too ill to sign, and never once taken to mean the Warden did not write it. She is the only person in the story who has been staring at the answer since before the answer existed.
cast.alibi: For 14 September 1998: in the Accounts Office with the door open, which is where she has been between 08:45 and 17:15 on every working day for thirty-six years, and which the whole building will confirm without being asked.
lies: 'Sundry Adjustments (Lights) is a rounding account. It's always been there.' CAUGHT IN ACTS I–III: it was opened on 31 December 1974 in her own hand, on a ruled-in column, and the balance of £4,180 4s 0d has not moved in ninety-six quarters.
'Nobody ever told me anything about the Nine Bells. I only do the figures.' CAUGHT IN ACT IV when she unfolds the back cover of the cash book on Rossport quay.
'I don't keep used ribbons, whatever would I want with used ribbons.' CAUGHT IN ACT IV: her own stationery ledger, rule 4, and a shelf of two hundred and forty docketed spools going back to 1968.
'I burned nothing. I was airing the courtyard.' CAUGHT IN ACT III, at 22:50, in her nightdress and coat, with the 1974 cash book in her hands and the fire not taking.
cast.arc: A whole character delivered in one accounting habit. The single most damning artefact in the accounts is in her handwriting, and the police spend a full day on her for embezzlement, and the memorandum that clears her is one of the seven weeded documents — so for four acts the only person the money points at is the woman holding the cashbox. She resigns on 2 November, hands over the memorandum on Rossport quay to the woman she has spent twenty-four years campaigning against, gives evidence to the Board by telephone from her sister's house in Ilberry because she cannot make herself come back into the building, and in the epilogue is granted immunity, keeps her pension, and never sets foot on the headland again. Her last line in the game: 'I want it minuted that I raised it. Once. In writing. It's in the file. It has always been in the file.'

cast.name: Dr Ivo Sandbach
cast.role: Conservation architect and project manager, Sandbach & Roule, for the conversion of Pilotage House into a heritage hotel. An outsider. Briskly charming, obsessed with the completion date, contemptuous of 'the paper people'.
cast.appearance: Big and soft-handed, six foot two, going heavy round the middle. Sandy hair receding, cut expensively in a town nobody here has been to. Ruddy and handsome in a bruised way; blue eyes; three days of stubble by Act III. Quilted olive gilet over a checked shirt, cord trousers, brand-new steel-toed boots that are not dirty until the night of the crowbar. Carries a hard hat and never wears it, a Nokia the size of a brick, and an A3 drawings tube with a photograph of two girls aged nine and twelve rolled inside it. CHARACTERISTIC EXPRESSION: cheerful, and about fifteen per cent too fast.
cast.personality: A man doing sums in his head while he talks to you. Genuinely knowledgeable about lime mortar and genuinely uninterested in anything that is not on the programme. Bullies with jokes. Sleeps in the site hut four nights a week and tells his wife it is the ferry.
cast.speechStyle: Programme language: 'we're out of float on that', 'that's a Tuesday problem'. Uses first names immediately and wrongly. Talks over people, apologises charmingly, does it again.
cast.motive: Sandbach & Roule is nine weeks from administration. Brannock is the only contract holding it up and the funding tranche releases on practical completion, 1 December. A reopened marine inquiry freezes the site as a place of interest and kills the firm, the house, and two sets of school fees.
cast.secret: He has been selling the Authority's dismounted brasswork — two Fresnel lens panels, the Ardent's binnacle, a hundred and forty kilos of fittings — to a dealer in Antwerp to cover a payroll gap, and falsifying the schedule of condition to hide it. About thirty thousand pounds. He is guilty of exactly the thing he appears guilty of and of nothing else whatsoever. What he does not know is that he keeps the only contemporaneous daily record in the building that the Warden does not control, and that it will convict her.
cast.alibi: For 14 September 1998: in Rossport with the structural engineer, in his own site diary, in his own handwriting, corroborated by an invoice — the cleanest alibi in the story, and it belongs to the man the player most wants to be guilty.
lies: 'Nothing leaves this site without a schedule entry. I'm Ministry-approved, for God's sake.' CAUGHT IN ACT III at two in the morning in the Lamp Room, and confirmed by the Antwerp dealer's shipping docket in the glovebox of his Discovery.
'I've never been up in that gallery. It's not in my scope.' CAUGHT IN ACT IV by his own site diary, items 41 and 63.

'The rail was made good under the programme.' CAUGHT IN ACT IV: item 63 reads 'at Warden's personal instruction, out of programme, no order no., not billed' — the sentence that puts a repair in a room the morning after a death.
'I've no idea what's in that crate. It's Rita's.' CAUGHT IN ACT III in the first four seconds.
cast.arc: Plot machinery in a coat until Act IV, when the machinery turns out to be load-bearing three separate times: his site diary is the hard outside witness to the gallery rail, his scaffolders removed the incinerator damper so the fire would not draw on the night of 26 October, and one of the two Fresnel panels he sold is the panel Wren needs to make the optic work. At four in the morning on 3 November he drives to Rossport and buys it back off the shipping agent with money he does not have, and hands it over wrapped in a fleece, and says nothing about it. He is charged with theft and false accounting, Sandbach & Roule goes into administration on 19 January 1999, and the conversion is completed by another firm. The one decent thing he does in nine days is enough to make him a person and not enough to save him, which is the correct outcome.

cast.name: Bram Aylward
cast.role: Introduces himself as a Ministry 'dissolution liaison'. Is in fact a recovery investigator for Kelbrooke & Hain, marine adjusters, acting for the successors to the 1974 reinsurers of the Pelagia.
cast.appearance: Lean and quick, five foot ten, dark hair cut short and neat, a young face with old eyes and a small chip out of the left front tooth. Clean-shaven, faintly nicked at the jaw. A charcoal single-breasted suit one grade better than anything else in the building, a navy raincoat, brown brogues entirely wrong for the weather and always wet. A hard-sided document case with a three-wheel combination lock, containing an Olympus OM-2, a folding copy-stand, and a letter from a widow in Grimsby dated 1994. CHARACTERISTIC EXPRESSION: friendly, alert, never quite still — the eyes taking an inventory of the room while the mouth is being pleasant.
cast.personality: Excellent company and structurally untrustworthy, and he knows it and has stopped minding. He is very good at this and it is the only thing he is good at. Buys the drinks. Remembers your supervisor's name. Never lies about a fact and never tells the truth about himself, and once Wren works out that rule he becomes the most useful person in the story and she still cannot use him.
cast.speechStyle: Light, quick, disarmingly frank about everything except his employer. Deflects with a question. Quotes figures to the penny from memory. When he finally tells the truth in Act III he does it in the flattest voice he has.
cast.motive: The 1975 reinsurance settlement was paid on a finding of pilot error. If that finding was procured by an authority that knew its own light was out, the syndicate's successors can reopen for fraudulent non-disclosure: £14.2 million at 1998 values, and a personal recovery fee for him of three point nine per cent, which he has already spent. He needs the truth to come out, which does not make him honest.
cast.secret: No Ministry ever heard of him. He has been in the building under a false name since 6 October and has already photographed one thousand one hundred documents — including two of the seven that Sabine weeded and Pike stole, meaning that in a briefcase in a Rossport guest house he has copies of documents Wren spends three acts hunting. In 1994 he closed a claim wrongly and a widow in Grimsby got nothing, and he carries her letter, and he does this now because he cannot stop.
cast.alibi: For 14 September 1998: at the Kelbrooke & Hain office in Liverpool, provable in ten seconds by a firm he will not name for two and a half acts — so for two and a half acts he has no alibi at all, by choice.
lies: 'Aylward, Ministry — dissolution liaison.' CAUGHT IN ACT I if the player is sharp: the Ministry staff circular in the Long Registry lists all four liaison officers by name, and his identification card is laser-printed on 90gsm, in 1998, in a building where every other card in the game was letterpressed in 1988.
'I only got here on Tuesday.' CAUGHT IN ACT I: the visitors' book, 6 October.
'I haven't photographed a thing. I wouldn't dare.' CAUGHT IN ACT III: thirty-one rolls of HP5, contact-printed, two frames of documents that no longer exist anywhere on earth.

He never once lies about a fact of the case. Everything he tells Wren is true, she is right not to trust him, and being right costs her a full day in Act II — which the game states plainly and does not apologise for.
cast.arc: Fixed from plot device to pressure: in Act III, with Rita arrested and the commission revoked, Bram's photographs are the only surviving images of two weeded documents, and he will trade them — for Wren's signed statement, which Kelbrooke & Hain will use to reopen the claim, which will freeze the archive as evidence and mean the Board sits without her and the pulper runs on 4 November. A genuine dilemma with a real ending consequence, resolvable three ways. Whatever she chooses, he is at the Board, at the back, in the good suit, taking notes; and in the epilogue Kelbrooke & Hain recover £9.1 million in 2003, of which the thirty-one families receive nothing, because they were never parties. Bram sends Wren a Christmas card every year for the rest of the series and she has never once opened one.

cast.name: DS Marren Iveson
cast.role: Detective Sergeant, Rossport. Two officers, one car, a district of four hundred square miles and a coroner's officer who does three days a week. The nearest thing to a police investigation this story is going to get.
cast.appearance: Broad and capable, five foot seven, dark hair scraped back into a short tail. Freckled across the nose and cheekbones; a broken nose set badly in 1983; grey eyes. Padded navy jacket over an off-the-peg suit, sensible boots, a wedding ring and a hair elastic on the same wrist. Notebook with a rubber band round it, kept in the left inside pocket, and a habit of writing while you are still talking. CHARACTERISTIC EXPRESSION: flat, unhurried, faintly sympathetic and entirely unmoved.
cast.personality: Neither obstructive nor stupid, which the genre rarely allows. Believes what she can put in front of a magistrate and nothing else. Treats Wren as a nineteen-year-old for three acts and as a competent professional witness from the moment she is handed a properly cited schedule of exhibits, and the switch is one of the most satisfying rewards in the game.
cast.speechStyle: Procedural, economical, occasionally very dry. 'That's an inference, that is. Bring me an object.' Reads documents aloud slowly while she thinks.
cast.motive: None; she is not a suspect. Her function is to be the wall the player's case has to be strong enough to stand against, and to say the sentence the whole game is built to earn.
cast.secret: She read the coroner's file on Cormac Sallow in early October, on her own time, because the fall bothered her — eleven minutes between the fall and the call, according to the pathologist's estimate of lividity, and a witness who typed a report about it four hours later. She raised it with her inspector and was told there was nothing in it. Her request slip is in the file, and Wren can find it in Act I and think nothing of it.
cast.alibi: Not applicable; on the mainland throughout.
lies: 'The coroner's file's closed and I've never laid eyes on it.' CAUGHT IN ACT I, if the player reads the whole file: her own request slip, dated 2 October, is stapled inside the back cover. She lies because she was told to drop it and does not want a nineteen-year-old repeating it in a corridor.
'This is a paper matter. There's no crime here.' CAUGHT IN ACT V, by the player, with a schedule of exhibits.
cast.arc: From the officer who arrests the wrong woman on 31 October to the officer who, on the morning of 3 November, tells Wren over the radio that an uncautioned confession heard on a rock in a gale is worth precisely nothing and that she should stop crying and go and do her job — the single most important line in the game, because it is the game's fair-play contract spoken aloud by someone with the power to enforce it. She takes the referral, wording and all, in interview room 2, and it is her name on the file that goes to the Crown Prosecution Service.

cast.name: Phyllida Halkett
cast.role: Senior Appraiser, National Records Conservancy. Wren's supervisor. Should have taken this commission herself and did not, because on 12 October she broke her hip in a stairwell at the Ilberry store. Reachable only from the GPO call box on Rossport quay, at low water, with a pocketful of ten-pence pieces. THE DIEGETIC HINT LINE.
cast.appearance: For four acts, a voice on a bakelite handset and a passport photograph clipped inside the cover of Wren's casebook: silver hair in a severe bob, reading glasses pushed up into it, a hawk's face, a mustard scarf. At the Board on 3 November she is present in person: tweed, a plaster cast to the hip, a stick in each hand, and a walking frame parked six feet away which she has refused to touch since Tuesday. CHARACTERISTIC EXPRESSION: eyebrows up, waiting for you to finish.
cast.personality: Twenty-nine years of appraisal has left her with total recall of procedure and a professional's horror of opinion. Will explain, at any length, at any hour, exactly what section 41 permits, how to certify a series, how to word an adverse report, what a warrant does and does not authorise, and what happens on 4 November if the certificate is not signed. Will not say one word about who did it. Says 'that's not a question for me' the way other people say 'no'.
cast.speechStyle: Dry, exact, patient, with pauses for the pips. Ends every call with 'have you eaten?' and rings off before the answer.
cast.motive: None. She is the game's conscience and its manual, and the reason the player is never stuck without being told anything a detective ought to work out.
cast.secret: She nominated Wren for this commission on 3 October — nine days before she fell. She has told Wren, and the Conservancy, and herself, that the hip is why an apprentice was sent alone to a dissolving archive with a dead man's letter in the file. It is not. She read Sallow's letter, disliked it intensely, believed the building would close ranks against anybody it recognised, and sent a stranger, exactly as he asked. She has not decided whether that was professional courage or the worst thing she has ever done, and she does not tell Wren until the Board Room steps.
cast.alibi: In traction in Ilberry Cottage Hospital from 12 October; before that, four hundred miles away.
lies: 'I sent you because I broke my hip, and for no other reason on earth.' CAUGHT IN ACT IV: the Conservancy's own commission minute, which Wren requisitions for a completely different purpose, shows the nomination dated 3 October and the fall dated 12 October.

'I have no view on it. That's not a question for me.' Repeated verbatim, forty or fifty times across nine days, in the face of increasingly desperate questions, and it is not a lie — it is the discipline the whole game is about, and the one time she breaks it, in Act V, the player will remember it for the rest of the series.
cast.arc: The voice in the call box that tells you how the machinery works and never once tells you what to think — the reason the player's deductions are the player's. On 3 November she gets herself onto the ferry on two sticks in a gale, sits at the back of the Board Room, and says nothing at all until it is over. On the steps, in the sun, she tells Wren why she really sent her, and asks whether she should have. The game does not give the player a way to answer.

cast.name: Cormac Sallow
cast.role: Lamp Superintendent of the Brannock Pilotage Authority 1958–1984. Dead before page one: fell from the Muniment gallery onto flagstones at approximately 10:24 on Monday 14 September 1998. The man whose last request is the entire plot.
