cast.appearance: Present only as a three-quarter oil in the Lamp Superintendents' frame in the Lamp Room, painted 1979 against a dark ground exactly like the Wardens on the Great Stair, and as one police photograph in the coroner's file that the game lets you look at once. Big-boned and heavy-shouldered, six foot one and stooped by the end; white hair in a brush cut; a face like a weathered cliff, deep-set brown eyes, a jaw that has been broken; enormous scarred hands with two fingers missing the top joints from a lantern gear in 1962. A knitted waistcoat over a collarless shirt, a hearing aid in the right ear with the cord tucked into the waistcoat. Painted expression: patient, faintly amused, waiting for you to catch up.
cast.personality: Reconstructed entirely from paper and from other people's grief: methodical, literal, kind in an undemonstrative way, incapable of exaggeration, and — the fatal quality — trusting of documents. He believed a wage sheet over the evidence of his own eyes because a wage sheet is a document and Cass Verge was a colleague.
cast.speechStyle: Heard only in his own writing: the 1975 inquiry transcript, thirty years of lamp reports, and one letter. Short sentences. No adjectives. Numbers wherever a number will do. The letter of 11 September 1998 is nine lines long, gives no explanation whatsoever, and ends 'I would be obliged if series 14/B were read by a stranger before it leaves this building.'
cast.motive: In early September 1998, sorting his retirement papers at 3 Coastguard Row, he found his own file copy of oil requisition R.755 — refused, stamped REFER WINTER REFIT, initialled p.p. — and recognised the hand that had made the initials, because he had watched it write for twenty-six years. He was in hospital for a hernia from 20 August to 10 October 1974 and had no idea until that morning what had been done while he was away.
cast.secret: He gave evidence for the Authority at the Rossport Inquiry in 1975 in good faith and helped to hang a dead man, and he found out about it at seventy-nine years of age, alone, at a kitchen table. He wrote to the Conservancy rather than the police or the newspapers because he was an institutional man to the bone and believed the right way to fix a record was to have somebody read it properly. He did not tell his daughter-in-law, or Rita, or anybody. He tried to tell Rita in August and she was too angry to listen, and she will carry that.
lies: ROSSPORT INQUIRY, 1975, Day 9, in answer to Sir Roderick Balgowan: 'Was the light exhibited on the night of 3 November?' — 'The light was not discontinued.' True, precise, and catastrophically misleading, and it is the sentence on which the finding rests. CAUGHT IN ACT II when Wren reads the transcript in the Long Registry and notices that a Lamp Superintendent answered a question about exhibition with an answer about administration.

ROSSPORT INQUIRY, 1975, Day 9: 'I have no knowledge of any requisition for oil being refused.' False, and honestly so — he had signed R.741 himself on 13 August and was under anaesthetic when it came back. CAUGHT IN ACTS III–IV when his own initials turn up on the front of a requisition he swore he had never seen. The most sympathetic lie in the game: a good man's memory failing, and a dead pilot paying for it for twenty-four years.
cast.arc: The absent protagonist. The entire game is one old man's requisition slip being filled, forty-three days late, by a stranger. His spectacles stay folded on the reading slope in the Muniment gallery north bay from Act II to the end and the player is never permitted to move them. In the epilogue his file copy of R.755 is exhibit 4 in the Board's schedule, his letter is bound at the front of the case file, and Notice to Mariners 74/119 is issued over the Conservancy's certificate with a footnote recording that the series was read at the request of Cormac Sallow, Lamp Superintendent, deceased. It is the only thanks anyone in the story ever gets.

clues.name: Wren's Water-Damaged Commission under s.41, Coastal Services Act 1997
clues.whatItProves: Teaches humidification, separation and blotting — skill 1, step zero — and establishes that Wren's entire authority in this building is a sheet of paper she can destroy by hurrying. Also fixes the clock: certification by 3 November or the archive is deemed valueless and pulped on the 4th.

clues.name: Visitors' Book, entry for Monday 14 September 1998
clues.whatItProves: C. SALLOW signed in at 08:56 and never signed out. The 'admitted by' column is initialled S.F-K., not H.P. and not O.V.
clues.misleadsToward: Ottoline Verge, who was on the wicket that morning and says so

clues.name: The Warden's Specimen Bundle: nine documents of 1974 'house style'
clues.whatItProves: Every document of the fatal period is signed A. FERRIER and carries, in 2H pencil in the lower left corner, the two-millimetre notation p.p. Shown voluntarily, at full readable resolution, inside the first thirty minutes, by the person it convicts.
clues.misleadsToward: none — it is the answer, offered as hospitality

clues.name: Ottoline's Requisition-Slip Lesson
clues.whatItProves: Teaches the p.p. notation as a boring clerical courtesy — 'if the Warden's out, her clerk initials it per procurationem, on behalf of' — from a woman who has no idea what she has just handed the player.

clues.name: Pike's Complaint about Docketing (the Ministry fold and the squared treasury tag)
clues.whatItProves: Establishes, as an old man's grievance and nothing else, that exactly one hand in the building endorses a folder on the outside third, upside down to the tag, and squares the tag tail-under, loop-left. Never repeated, never journalled, never prompted again.
clues.misleadsToward: Pike, as a crank with a grudge

clues.name: Accident Report on the death of C. Sallow, typed 16:50, 14 September 1998
clues.whatItProves: The only document in 187 years of the Authority's records signed by Sabine Ferrier-Kyne in her own name. Typed on the Imperial 66. Docketed the Ministry way, upside down to the tag. The player reads it in the first hour and reads the signature as an administrator doing her duty.

clues.name: DS Iveson's File Request Slip, 2 October 1998
clues.foundIn: The Reading Room, stapled inside the back cover of the coroner's file
clues.whatItProves: A serving detective sergeant pulled the Sallow file on her own initiative three weeks before Wren arrived, and was told there was nothing in it. Catches Iveson's only lie and tells the player, early, that somebody with a warrant card was already uneasy.

clues.name: Schedule of Outstanding Liabilities, Item 14: Superannuation Arrears, FERRIER-KYNE, S.
clues.whatItProves: A £2,140 4s pension arrears claim, filed March 1998, in which Sabine asserts under her own signature that her reckonable service runs from 1959. It is the only document in existence in which she claims to have been working in this building in 1974. The player is meant to cross it off in the first hour, and does.

clues.name: Four Typewriter Specimen Sheets and the 'a'-Clogging Curve
clues.foundIn: The Binding Room bench (typed on machines in the Warden's Office, Rolls Room, Registry and Accounts)
clues.whatItProves: Skill 2, taught: Imperial 66 (clogged a, comma 0.4mm high, broken y descender); Underwood 5 (e riding 0.3mm high, wandering 3); Olivetti Lettera 32 (grey doubling, chipped l); Remington Noiseless (heavy g, capitals dropping 0.2mm). The Imperial's a has been filling since 1961 at a plottable rate, which turns the machine into a clock.

clues.name: The Pitney Postmaster Franking Meter and its Descending Register
clues.whatItProves: Skill 4, taught, on a physical object the player winds, opens and reads under warrant: a machine that has recorded, without opinion or ambition, every penny of postage the Authority has spent since 1961, and which nobody has ever conceived of as a witness.

clues.name: Scorched Carbon of Notice to Mariners 74/119, drafted 15 August 1974
clues.foundIn: The Courtyard Incinerator, ash grate, after rain
clues.whatItProves: MARINERS ARE ADVISED THAT THE LIGHT EXHIBITED FROM THE NINE BELLS BEACON MAY NOT BE RELIED UPON UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE. A warning was written on 15 August 1974. It also proves somebody was still trying to destroy it at 01:20 on 27 October 1998.
clues.misleadsToward: Halvard Pike, who has courtyard keys and no alibi

clues.name: Site Diary item 41: incinerator chimney damper removed, 2 September 1998
clues.whatItProves: The flue would not draw, which is why the burning failed and the carbon survived. The building's own dissolution saved the document — and Sandbach's diary, the one daily record the Warden does not control, enters the game as a witness in Act I so that its Act IV use is not a convenience.

clues.name: Register of Notices Issued, 1974
clues.whatItProves: The sequence runs 74/117, 74/118, 74/120. No cancellation minute, no reallocation, no note. A number was used and then unused.

clues.name: Duplicating Book, 15 August 1974 (Reprax 12 impression counter)
clues.whatItProves: Counter 41,882 to 42,319 — an advance of 437 against 223 impressions logged. Two hundred and fourteen copies of a document that officially does not exist were physically produced on 15 August 1974. Distribution list Schedule D has 214 addressees.

clues.name: Notices to Mariners Distribution List, Schedule D
clues.whatItProves: Two hundred and fourteen addressees in statutory precedence. No. 1 is 'The Keeper, Nine Bells Beacon — per relief boatman, Cardew Post Office, tel. Cardew 4471.' The light is told about itself first.

clues.name: Forty-Seven Retyped Index Cards (raised lower-case 'e')
clues.whatItProves: Cards retyped on the Underwood 5 on card stock not manufactured before 1987. Sorting by stock, ribbon and typeface yields seven accession numbers in series 14/B that exist as cards and no longer exist as paper — the want-list for Acts III and IV. Weeding a file takes an afternoon; weeding an index takes a fortnight; nobody did it.
clues.misleadsToward: Sabine's 1989 reboxing memorandum, which looks like the whole answer

clues.name: Memorandum W/O 89/2, 'Rationalisation and Reboxing of Series 14/B'
clues.whatItProves: Sabine ordered the reboxing openly, in daylight, in her own name, in 1989, and its attached schedule lists twenty-three items in box 17 against seventeen now present. It is a cover-up of a cover-up, done clumsily and legibly, which is exactly why it reads as the entire crime.
clues.misleadsToward: Sabine — correctly, for entirely the wrong crime, three acts early

clues.name: Wren's Own Requisition Stubs 2271, 2283, 2291 and 2302
clues.foundIn: Wren's casebook, Binding Room (stubs in the Registry stub book)
clues.whatItProves: Of thirty-one requisitions across nine days, four came back substituted, not traced, or razored. Standing Order 7, printed on the back of every slip, routes every reader's slip through the Warden's pigeonhole for countersignature. The kindness was the gate, and the evidence of the steering is in the victim's own handwriting from the first morning. Read as a set in Act IV, the negative space draws the shape of the crime.
clues.misleadsToward: Halvard Pike, who runs the tubes and the trolley

clues.name: Cormac Sallow's Evidence, Rossport Inquiry 1975, Day 9
clues.foundIn: The Long Registry, bound inquiry transcripts
clues.whatItProves: Asked whether the light was exhibited on 3 November, the Lamp Superintendent answered 'the light was not discontinued' — an administrative answer to an operational question, true and catastrophic. Also: 'I have no knowledge of any requisition being refused', which his own initials will contradict in Act III.
clues.misleadsToward: Sallow as an Authority man who lied for his employer

clues.name: Warden's Order Book: closing hours of every working day since 1946
clues.foundIn: The Registry (working copy) and the strongroom door
clues.whatItProves: Supplies the three settings for the Chubb timelock movements — different hours for 1974, 1998 and Saturdays. Opens the strongroom, and locks Wren inside it.

clues.name: Page Two of Notice 74/119, on blue-black flimsy
clues.foundIn: The Strongroom, japanned deed box stencilled A. FERRIER, WARDEN, bottom shelf
clues.whatItProves: The second sheet of the notice whose first sheet is ash — including the phrase 'until oil supply is restored and the No. 2 vaporiser renewed', which names the mechanical fault and therefore ties the notice to Sallow's report and to the refused requisitions.
clues.misleadsToward: Absalom Ferrier, whose name is on the box

clues.name: Cormac Sallow's Spectacles, folded on the reading slope
clues.foundIn: The Muniment Gallery, north bay, behind the map presses
clues.whatItProves: He took them off. A man reading does not fold his spectacles; a man standing up to talk to somebody does. Untouched for six weeks in a room the police walked through twice. The player may never move them.

clues.name: Dust Reference Jar 6 (gallery north bay) against Coroner's Exhibit 4 (turn-ups)
clues.foundIn: The Binding Room bench; sample taken in the Muniment Gallery, exhibit released by the coroner's officer
clues.whatItProves: WHERE, two acts before WHO. French chalk, beeswax and a particular salt bloom occur in exactly one room in the building. Sallow was not at the 14/B shelving where his box came from; he was in the dead corner behind the map presses, where two people go to have a conversation nobody hears. The same chalk-wax is later found in the ribbon well and platen knob of the Imperial 66 in the Warden's Office.
clues.misleadsToward: none — it names a room, and the room names nobody yet

clues.name: The Deakin Letter, dated 4 March 1975
clues.foundIn: The Lamp Room, Rita's campaign file
clues.whatItProves: Appears to be a crewman's confession that the beacon was dark and the crew were told to say nothing — and appears, for one act, to end the case. Fails authentication on two of five steps: Ardwell Bond paper, unissued before June 1981, and a Cardew sorting-office frank, last struck 30 September 1972. Third tell for the thorough: a nylon ribbon on an Adler Gabriele, and an Adler Gabriele in Rita's locker.
clues.misleadsToward: first the Authority, then — devastatingly — Rita Tain, and through her the entire true proposition that the light was out

clues.name: Deposition of Norah Feaver (1975) against the Admiralty List of Lights, 1974
clues.whatItProves: Nine Bells: Fl(3) W 20s. Cadran Point, nine miles SSE: Fl(3) W 15s. The honest surviving witness genuinely saw three flashes and was telling the exact truth; she saw Cadran. For twenty-four years the strongest evidence that the beacon was burning was a frightened nineteen-year-old whom nobody ever asked to count the seconds.
clues.misleadsToward: 'the light was clearly exhibited' — the single load-bearing error of the 1975 finding

clues.name: Three Registered Surveys of the Nine Bells Approach (1948, 1974 buoyage, 1998)
clues.whatItProves: The Rossport Inquiry drew the Pelagia's reconstructed track on the 1948 sheet. Registered on triangulation marks against the 1974 buoyage, she is not where the finding says she was: she is precisely on the line a competent pilot would steer. Emrys Tain is exonerated by tracing paper and a pair of dividers. The same registration reveals a chamber under the north undercroft absent from every plan after 1975.

clues.name: Works Order 75/188, June 1975: 'seal chamber, damp'
clues.foundIn: The Undercroft, north wall (order in the Long Registry works file)
clues.whatItProves: The Tide Room was bricked up nine months after the wreck, in cement twenty-three years younger than the wall around it, on an order initialled p.p. — the last p.p. anyone ever wrote in this building.

clues.name: Marigraph Drum 1974/44, Kelvin & White stilling-well tide gauge
clues.whatItProves: A pen on a clockwork drum that has scratched the height of the sea onto smoked paper since 1908 without an opinion in its head, unread since 1975, which the player must re-ink, re-hang, wind and start before it will testify. Drum 44 shows a surge of 1.4m above prediction on the night of 3 November 1974: Tain had 4.2m over the Sowens shoal. The Inquiry's central assumption about the tide is simply wrong, and was wrong in a machine's handwriting the whole time.

clues.name: Rossport Inquiry: List of Persons Considered and Not Called, 1975
clues.foundIn: The Tide Room, bundle of the Inquiry's returned working papers, never accessioned
clues.whatItProves: No. 29: 'Mrs O. Verge — wife of relief keeper — no direct knowledge — not called', with a tick in the margin in Ottoline's own hand. No. 33: 'Miss S. Ferrier — the Warden's private secretary — no official capacity — not called.' The erasure exists in ink, in the assessor's own file, and the document is not in the index because it was never accessioned — which is why it is the only thing in the building nobody could have weeded.
clues.misleadsToward: none — this is the thematic keystone

clues.name: Oil Requisition Book, Nine Bells, 1966–1980
clues.whatItProves: R.741 (13 Aug), R.748 (9 Sep) and R.755 (7 Oct) 1974, each stamped REQUISITION NOT SANCTIONED — REFER WINTER REFIT, each initialled p.p. Removed by Pike in 1985 under Ministry Circular 12/85, four years before Sabine came looking for it.
clues.misleadsToward: Absalom Ferrier, whose initials the stamp bears

clues.name: Lamp Superintendent's Report, 15 August 1974
clues.whatItProves: Sallow's own report: No. 2 vaporiser cracked, reserve oil ninety gallons, 'light cannot be maintained beyond the end of the month'. Signed C. SALLOW. It is the document that caused Notice 74/119 to be drafted on the same day, and it is the document that hangs his 1975 evidence.

clues.name: Despatch Docket, Notices to Mariners, 16 August 1974
clues.whatItProves: The contents docket for the fortnightly batch lists 74/117, 74/118 and 74/119. 74/119 is struck through — not erased, not typed over, ruled out in 2H pencil — and initialled p.p. The moment of decision, in graphite, with a date on it. Foot of the docket, in the clerk's hand: '214 @ 4d — £3 11s 4d.'

clues.name: Franking Meter Descending Register against the Post Book, 16 August 1974
clues.foundIn: The Post Room (meter and post book); recharge readings in the Meter Card Book
clues.whatItProves: Cross-totalled between the recharges of 2 August and 4 September, the 16 August despatch cost £3 11s 0d — 852 pence, 213 impressions at fourpence — against a docket, a post book and a distribution list that all say 214. One envelope in that batch was never franked and never posted, and Schedule D No. 1 is the Keeper of the Nine Bells, care of the call box at Cardew. Fourpence, and thirty-one lives.

clues.name: The Reconciliation: Light Dues Ledger + Oil Requisition Book + Keeper's Wage Sheets, 1 July–31 December 1974
clues.whatItProves: Filled column by column, week by week, on a Conservancy reconciliation form. Dues collected every week. Wages paid every week. Oil drawn 24 August and never again. Seventy-one days; ten complete dues weeks; 1,182 vessels charged £4,180 4s 0d for a light that was not burning; £200 4s 0d paid over eleven weeks to a keeper who was not there. No hint, no highlight, no chime. The third column simply refuses to agree.
clues.misleadsToward: none — this is the game's thesis executed as a mechanic

clues.name: 'Sundry Adjustments (Lights)', opened 31 December 1974
clues.foundIn: The Accounts Office, 1974 cash book (recovered from the incinerator, 30 October)
clues.whatItProves: A column ruled in by hand into which £4,180 4s 0d disappeared and has been carried forward, untouched and unqueried, for ninety-six quarters. The sum is exactly the dues collected on a dark light.
clues.misleadsToward: Enid Charnock, embezzlement — the police spend a full day on it

clues.name: Sallow's File Copy of Oil Requisition R.755
clues.foundIn: Rita's shed at the slipway, in three unopened boxes of Cormac Sallow's effects
clues.whatItProves: The object that made a seventy-nine-year-old man write to a stranger: his own copy of a refused requisition, initialled p.p. in a hand he had watched write for twenty-six years. Also bears his own signature on the front, which destroys his 1975 evidence and breaks Rita, who was too angry to listen to him in August.

clues.name: Forty-Eight Documents Signed 'A. Ferrier', 2 August–30 November 1974
clues.foundIn: The Chart Loft light table (drawn from four independent custodies: the strongroom, Pike's cottage, Enid's ledgers and Ottoline's tin)
clues.whatItProves: Sorted signed against p.p., the answer is 41 and 0: every document from 11 August to 3 November 1974 is per procurationem. Seven decoys, dated 2–10 August and 18 November onward, are a genuine and shaky man's hand and fix the boundary dates unaided. The signature is not forged; it is scrupulously legal, and no rule anywhere required anybody to write down who made it.
clues.misleadsToward: none — this is the twist, and the player performs it rather than being told it

clues.name: Dr Munn's Locum Mileage Claims, August–November 1974
clues.foundIn: The Accounts Office, medical attendance file
clues.whatItProves: Brannock House, fourteen miles, twice weekly, from 12 August 1974 — an expense claim, kept for tax, that incidentally documents a man's collapse.

clues.name: Nurse Kilbride's Visit Ledger, 1974
clues.foundIn: Brannock House, former sickroom (now a paint store)
clues.whatItProves: '12.8.74 — pt. hemiplegic R side, no speech, cannot hold pen, wife present.' Absalom Ferrier signed nothing after 11 August 1974 because he physically could not.

clues.name: Mirror Offsets of the Razored Order Book Leaves, 11 Aug–3 Nov 1974
clues.foundIn: The Muniment Room, Warden's Order Book 1972–1976
clues.whatItProves: The leaves were taken out at the gutter with a razor in 1989, but fifteen years of pressure left their ink in mirror image on the facing pages, readable under raking light with a shaving mirror. Recovers the deferment of the relief keeper, two of the three refusals, and the instruction to continue the wages.

clues.name: Cass Verge's Deferment Letter, 18 August 1974
clues.foundIn: Ottoline's cottage, 4 Coastguard Row, a biscuit tin on the dresser
clues.whatItProves: 'Your autumn residence at the Nine Bells is deferred pending refit. Wages will continue. You will not discuss this with the Lamp Superintendent or with any other officer.' Initialled p.p. The order that emptied the rock, kept for twenty-four years by a widow who thought she was protecting the wrong man.
clues.misleadsToward: Absalom Ferrier — which is precisely what Ottoline has believed since 1975

clues.name: Memorandum, Warden's Office to Cashier, 6 November 1974
clues.foundIn: Rossport Quay, folded inside the back cover of the 1974 cash book in Enid Charnock's shopping bag
clues.whatItProves: 'The Nine Bells oil column is to be carried to Sundry Adjustments (Lights) pending refit.' Initialled p.p., dated three days after the wreck. Clears Enid entirely and proves the concealment was ordered from the Warden's Office after the ship was on the rocks.
clues.misleadsToward: none — it is the document that turns a catastrophe into a cover-up

clues.name: Night Plug-Log, Sunday 3 November 1974
clues.whatItProves: Reconstructed by re-patching the twelve-line board: 22:34 IN, Rossport Coastguard to extension 2, six minutes; 22:41 OUT, extension 2 to Cardew 4471, four minutes, no answer; then 23:06, 23:11, 23:19 — the disaster hour. Extension 2 is the Warden's Office, on a Sunday night, and Cardew 4471 is the public call box forty yards from the relief keeper's front door.
clues.misleadsToward: Denzil Kyte, the nineteen-year-old night clerk, who logged it and left in 1976

clues.name: GPO Itemised Trunk Account, Quarter 4, 1974
clues.whatItProves: '3.11.74 — CARDEW — 22.41 — 4 min — 1s 9d', initialled EC. An outside record, kept by strangers for money, about which nobody in Pilotage House had a vote. It authenticates the plug-log the Board would otherwise strike as self-serving.

clues.name: Petty Cash Travel Voucher, 4 November 1974
clues.foundIn: The Accounts Office, petty cash box 1974
clues.whatItProves: 'S. Ferrier — Brannock to Cardew, return — 3s 6d — urgent, on the Warden's instruction.' The morning after thirty-one people drowned, a woman with no official capacity took a car to the village where the relief keeper lived, and claimed the fare.

clues.name: Naismith's Bank Letter, 15 August 1974
clues.whatItProves: No further facility. The Authority was approximately four months from insolvency on the day Notice 74/119 was written and the first oil requisition refused. Motive, in a bank manager's handwriting.

clues.name: Ministry Quinquennial Review of Pilotage Authorities, notice of 22 July 1974
clues.whatItProves: An authority found without an effective Warden was to be abolished, its officers dismissed and its records dispersed. The second half of the motive, six weeks before the stroke.

clues.name: Charter of the Brannock Pilotage Authority, 1811, Article 9
clues.whatItProves: 'The said office of Warden shall be holden by a man of full age.' Never amended in 187 years. The reason a competent woman running an institution had to sign on behalf of an unconscious one — the contempt and the alibi in the same clause.

clues.name: The Imperial 66 'a'-Occlusion Curve Applied
clues.whatItProves: Skill 2 escalated: the 1974 refusals sit at partial occlusion on the plotted curve, the 1998 accident report and the relabelled box 17 sit at full. Same machine, same room, twenty-four years apart, and the machine can be produced in evidence.

clues.name: Used Ribbon Spool, Imperial 66, September 1998
clues.foundIn: The Stationery Store (Enid's rule 4: no new ribbon issued until the used spool is returned)
clues.whatItProves: Read backwards under magnification, in unbroken sequence with no ribbon change between: 12.9.98, 'I know what you mean to send. Please do not send it. There is nothing in it that can help anybody now. S.' — never posted — and then the accident report of 14 September. She knew what Sallow intended two days before he died, and has denied it in writing three times.

clues.name: Site Diary items 41 and 63: the Muniment gallery rail
clues.whatItProves: 2 September: 'gallery rail nth bay, baluster 3 loose, made safe pending order.' 15 September: 'gallery rail nth bay made good at Warden's personal instruction, out of programme, no order no., not billed.' The rail a man went over was known to be defective, and was quietly repaired the next morning, off the books, by the one person who could not order it without leaving a trace anywhere else.
clues.misleadsToward: Ivo Sandbach, right up until the reader notices whose instruction it was

clues.name: Gallery Time-Switch Counter and the Fuel & Light Book, 14 September 1998
clues.foundIn: The Muniment Gallery (switch) and the Accounts Office (book)
clues.whatItProves: The north bay has no daylight and is lit by a twenty-minute spring time-switch with a counter read at lock-up and charged to the Lights account. Eleven windings on 14 September — 220 minutes of light — for a visit that lasted 88 minutes, the last of them logged by the caretaker at 17:40, seven hours after Sallow died and fifty minutes after the accident report was typed.

clues.name: Duplicating Book, 14 September 1998 (Reprax 12 counter)
clues.whatItProves: Counter advanced 41 against 12 logged. Twenty-nine unaccounted impressions on the day of the death, in a room whose book is Pike's and whose keeper was nine miles away on the ferry.
clues.misleadsToward: Halvard Pike, whose book it is

clues.name: Rossport Ferry Booking Book, Monday 14 September 1998
clues.whatItProves: H. PIKE, out 08:15, return 17:40. Pike was off the headland for the whole of the relevant period: he did not work the counter, did not issue slip R98/2211, and did not run twenty-nine Reprax impressions. The clue that clears the game's obvious suspect also identifies who must have done the counter work instead.

clues.name: Reading-Room Requisition Slip R98/2211, 09:10, 14 September 1998
clues.foundIn: The Registry, requisition stub book (pink carbon)
clues.whatItProves: C. SALLOW requisitions series 14/B box 17; 'issued by' column initialled S.F-K. With the ferry book, it places the Warden at the counter, and therefore in the strongroom and on the gallery stair, on a morning she says she spent in the Board Room. The first hard object.
clues.misleadsToward: nothing at all in Act I, where the player sees it and turns the page

clues.name: The Warden's Board of Dissolution Working File
clues.whatItProves: Twenty-six Reprax copies of the contents of series 14/B box 17, correctly foliated, correctly indexed, docketed the Ministry way, four of which are copies of documents no longer in box 17. She copied the evidence, destroyed the originals and filed the copies, because destruction is the one act an archivist cannot perform. Twenty-six copies plus three of the accident report is twenty-nine.
clues.misleadsToward: none — the character kills the character

clues.name: Series 14/B Box 17, relabelled and reshelved
clues.whatItProves: A box requisitioned at 09:10 on 14 September with no return entry against the slip, standing on its shelf behind a timelock the Warden alone can set, wearing a new label typed on the Imperial 66 at full 'a' occlusion. A box came home that was never sent home.

clues.name: Nine Bells Keeper's Log, final entry 24 August 1974
clues.foundIn: The Nine Bells Beacon, Oil Store
clues.whatItProves: '22.10. No. 2 vapor. cracked. Oil out. Light down. Nothing more to be done here.' The independent, non-Authority record that authenticates the refused requisitions and fixes the hour the beacon died. On the reverse of the last page, in pencil: tea, boot polish, a birthday card for Nan.

clues.name: The Kestrel Bequest: bank mandate, trust deed and standing-order schedule
clues.foundIn: The Nine Bells Beacon, Lantern Room (handed over by Sabine on the stair)
clues.whatItProves: Thirty-one index-linked monthly standing orders established 4 April 1977 out of Isobel Ferrier's legacy, through Mowbray & Slee of Rossport, paid for twenty-one years from an account no auditor queried because the sums were too small to be interesting. Matched against the Pelagia manifest, thirty are the dependants of the drowned. The thirty-first is M. TAIN.
clues.misleadsToward: none — the emotional detonation, and the strongest single item of consciousness of guilt in the file

clues.name: Conservancy Commission Minute, 3 October 1998
clues.foundIn: Wren's own commission file (requisitioned for an unrelated procedural reason)
clues.whatItProves: Phyllida Halkett nominated Wren nine days before she broke her hip. The supervisor did not send an apprentice by accident; she sent a stranger, because a dead man asked for one.

logline: In the autumn of 1998 a nineteen-year-old apprentice archivist is sent alone to appraise the records of a dissolving coastal pilotage authority in the nine days before they are pulped, and proves that the shipwreck which drowned thirty-one people in 1974 was caused not by a drunken pilot but by a safety notice that was written, approved and never sent — signed, lawfully and invisibly, by a hand the institution refused to let have a name.

protagonist.name: Wren Adare
protagonist.background: Second-year apprentice conservator, National Records Conservancy, Ilberry regional store. Raised in a council flat over a launderette in Ilberry by a mother who cleaned offices at night; left school at sixteen with five O-levels and no money and got the Conservancy apprenticeship because a librarian filled in the form for her. Two years of paper: washing, deacidifying, humidifying, leaf-casting, and eleven months on a single water-damaged parish register that taught her patience the hard way. She is not a plucky amateur sleuth. She is a professional reader of paper, which is a far stranger and more dangerous skill: she can date a document by its staple corrosion, tell a carbon from a photocopy at arm's length across a room, read an erased pencil line by raking light, and knows that the most incriminating object in any building is not the safe but the postage register. This is her first solo commission, and she is holding a legal instrument that lets a teenager open a strongroom a Warden cannot.
protagonist.voice: Flat Ilberry vowels, no charm, and a habit of correcting people's dates out loud that has cost her every friendship she has ever nearly had. Speaks in numbered points when nervous. Says 'that's not a document, that's a claim' the way other people say hello. Writes everything down in a wire-bound casebook with a citation column she rules herself, obsessively, in pencil — the player's evidence board, and, by Act IV, the most important exhibit in the case. Apologises constantly for things that are not her fault and never once for the things that are. When she is frightened she gets more precise, not less, and the game shows this by tightening her prose.
protagonist.flaw: She trusts institutions to be honest if the filing is honest. She believes — genuinely, structurally, the way other people believe in God — that a properly kept record cannot lie, and that if you follow procedure exactly the truth arrives on its own. Her flaw is the exact mirror of the culprit's: Sabine used a perfectly kept archive to disappear inside, and Wren has to learn that a perfectly kept archive can be the most complete lie in the world. Her secondary flaw is a physical one and the game makes her pay it in cash: she is genuinely, unglamorously terrified of open water, and the last document is nine miles offshore in a tower.
protagonist.whyHere: Because a dead man asked for a stranger. Cormac Sallow's letter of 11 September reached the Conservancy on 1 October; Phyllida Halkett, Senior Appraiser, nominated Wren on 3 October and broke her hip on the 12th, and has let everyone including Wren believe the hip was the reason. Wren cannot leave, and the reason is paper: her commission under section 41 obliges her to certify every series before dissolution on 3 November, and if she walks out uncertified the entire archive is deemed valueless and goes to the pulper on 4 November — twenty-four years of evidence destroyed lawfully, by clerical default. The ferry runs twice a week and the causeway floods. Everyone in the building knows both of those facts. Somebody is counting on them.

setting.place: Pilotage House, Brannock Head — a slate-and-granite records fortress on a headland at the mouth of Ivory Sound, seat of the Brannock Pilotage Authority (chartered 1811, dissolved by statute with effect from 1 December 1998). Six hundred feet of shelving, 187 years of pilotage logs, light-dues ledgers, wreck registers and inquiry files, a four-hundred-drawer card index, a pneumatic tube system, a twelve-line plug switchboard, a Chubb three-movement timelock strongroom, a Reprax 12 duplicator, four office typewriters with four distinct sets of injuries, a franking meter, an incinerator in the courtyard and, walled up under the north undercroft since June 1975, a tide gauge that has been telling the truth to nobody since 1908. Nine miles offshore, on its reef, stands the Nine Bells Beacon: a hundred and twelve feet of granite, a clockwork optic, an oil store and a dead lantern.
setting.era: Monday 26 October to Tuesday 3 November 1998 — nine days — with the whole weight of the case sitting in the eighty-four days between Sunday 11 August and Sunday 3 November 1974. Pre-digital and proud of it: nothing here can be searched with a keyword; everything must be walked to, requisitioned by slip, waited for, and read. The 1998 half of the game is bakelite, carbon paper, India rubber, sealing wax and a fax machine; the 1974 half is pounds, shillings and pence, four-penny stamps and a Charter written when the Prince Regent was on the throne.
setting.weather: North Atlantic autumn, escalating on a nine-day curve the player can feel without a timer. Acts I–II: grey, still, papery, rain on glass, dust hanging in a shaft of north light. Act III: streaming windows, a sixty-mile southwesterly, the causeway going under twice a day. Act IV: horizontal rain, a burning cottage on a black hill, the telephone line down and the sea getting up to storm force 10. Act V: the gale blows itself out overnight on the rock and 3 November 1998 dawns hard and blue and cold — the only fully sunlit day in the game, and the anniversary.
setting.history: Chartered 1811 to license pilots and levy dues on every vessel entering Ivory Sound. The Nine Bells Beacon first exhibited 1834, re-optic'd 1908 with a clockwork Fresnel showing Fl(3) W 20s. Nine miles south-south-east, Cadran Point shows Fl(3) W 15s, and has since 1911, and the difference between those two numbers is the difference between an accident and a crime. On the night of Sunday 3 November 1974 the coastal motor vessel Pelagia, inbound for Rossport with 118 aboard, steered for a light that was not there and went onto the reef at 23:04; thirty-one people drowned, among them the pilot, Emrys Tain, who was blamed for it in 1975 on the strength of a hip flask recovered from a body. Wardens: Absalom Ferrier 1961–1976 (incapacitated 11 August 1974 to 18 November 1974, a fact recorded nowhere); Gethin Rowe 1979–1991; Sabine Ferrier-Kyne 1991–1998. Half the building is now a working archive and half of it is a construction site: Sandbach & Roule, Conservation Architects, are converting Pilotage House into a heritage hotel with a hard completion date of 1 December, and the strip-out programme is pinned to the site hut wall, room by room, day by day.
setting.whyIsolated: Three locks, all of them mundane and all of them legal. Geography: the coast road washed out in the 1993 storms and was never rebuilt, so Brannock Head is reached by the Rossport ferry, twice a week, Mondays and Thursdays, or across a causeway passable for about two hours either side of low water — and both of those close in a gale. Law: Wren's commission under section 41 obliges her to certify every series in situ before dissolution; if she leaves uncertified the archive is deemed valueless and lawfully pulped on 4 November. Time: the Board of Dissolution sits on 3 November 1998, which is the twenty-fourth anniversary of the wreck, because somebody thought it was tidy. The isolation is not a device; it is a filing deadline, and it is the most frightening thing in the building.

solution.culprit: Sabine Ferrier-Kyne, 58, Warden of the Brannock Pilotage Authority — culpable in 1974 of the administrative decisions that darkened the Nine Bells and of twenty-four years of concealment, and in 1998 of the unlawful killing of Cormac Sallow.
solution.how: 1974: On Sunday 11 August her father, Warden Absalom Ferrier, suffered a cerebral haemorrhage and never signed anything again for ninety-nine days. The Authority was four months from insolvency, the bank refused further facility on 15 August, and the Ministry's quinquennial review was sitting: an authority discovered to have no effective Warden would have been abolished. So his thirty-four-year-old unpaid private secretary ran it, and signed every one of the forty-one documents of the fatal period 'A. Ferrier' with a two-millimetre pencil 'p.p.' beside it, exactly as Standing Order 4 permitted and Article 9 of the Charter of 1811 required, because that Article reserved the office to 'a man of full age'. On 15 August, on Cormac Sallow's report that the No. 2 vaporiser was cracked and the reserve oil down to ninety gallons, she drafted Notice to Mariners 74/119, had 214 copies run off on the Reprax, and refused oil requisition R.741 to the winter refit. On 16 August she ruled 74/119 out of the despatch docket in pencil and initialled it p.p.; 213 envelopes were franked and one — Schedule D No. 1, the Keeper of the Nine Bells, care of the call box at Cardew — was never posted at all. On 18 August she deferred the relief keeper's autumn residence with wages continuing, so that the rock was empty and Accounts would ask nothing. She refused R.748 on 9 September and R.755 on 7 October. She went on collecting the light dues throughout, because stopping them would have raised a question. At 21:10 on Saturday 24 August the last oil burned out and the Nine Bells went dark for seventy-one days. At 22:34 on Sunday 3 November the Rossport coastguard rang extension 2 to ask whether the beacon was exhibiting; at 22:41 she rang Cardew 4471 and let it ring for four minutes at a relief keeper who was in the Ship Inn; at 23:04 the Pelagia struck. On 6 November she instructed the Cashier to carry the empty oil column to sundries pending refit. 1998: on 8 September she saw Cormac Sallow's requisition slip for series 14/B box 17 pass through her countersignature pigeonhole; on 12 September she typed him a letter begging him not to send what he meant to send, and did not post it; on Monday 14 September, with the Chief Clerk on the Rossport ferry, she worked the registry counter herself, carried box 17 up to the Muniment gallery, and argued with him for forty minutes in the north bay behind the map presses. He refused. She took the folder; he took hold of it; he went backwards over a rail she knew had been loose since 2 September. She stood there for eleven minutes. Then she telephoned Rossport, and that afternoon photocopied twenty-six sheets on the Reprax, removed four documents, relabelled and reshelved the box behind a timelock only she could set, had the rail repaired the next morning off the programme, and typed the accident report at ten to five and signed it in her own name for the first time in her life.
solution.why: Because she was the only competent person left and she was not allowed to exist. In 1974 she was thirty-four, unpaid, untitled and running a bankrupt institution that would have been abolished if the Ministry had learned it was rudderless — and the Charter would not let her sign her own name to a single decision she made. She refused the oil and held the notice because there was no money until the winter refit and she intended, genuinely, to fix the light properly then. Then thirty-one people drowned, and because officially she had never been there, the Rossport Inquiry could not call her, question her, or list her among those present. The institution that had spent her whole life refusing to write her name down provided, in the one moment it mattered, a perfect alibi, and she took it. She has spent twenty-four years becoming a Warden who does everything correctly and paying thirty-one anonymous annuities out of her mother's money. In September 1998 she was a fortnight from appointment to the National Maritime Heritage Board — the first title she would ever have held in her own right — and one living man could still recognise her 1974 hand. The crime and the grievance are the same fact. The contempt that erased her is the mechanism that acquitted her, and she knows it, and she has never once said so out loud until four o'clock in the morning on a rock in a gale.
provingChain: LINK 1 — PRESENCE (1998). Requisition slip R98/2211, 09:10, 14 September, series 14/B box 17, 'issued by' initialled S.F-K., corroborated by the Rossport ferry booking book placing the Chief Clerk off the headland from 08:15 to 17:40, and by the gallery time-switch counter recording eleven windings for an eighty-eight-minute visit. Counter-evidence rebutted: her Board Room alibi collapses on Sandbach's site diary, which puts the quantity surveyor's meeting on the 15th.

LINK 2 — MEANS AND OPPORTUNITY (1998). Site diary item 41 (2 September: gallery rail north bay, baluster 3 loose, made safe pending order) and item 63 (15 September: made good at the Warden's personal instruction, out of programme, no order number, not billed). The defect was known; the repair was ordered off the books by the one person in the building who could not order anything else without leaving a trace. Corroborated by dust reference jar 6 against coroner's exhibit 4 — chalk-wax and salt bloom from the north bay behind the map presses, and the same chalk-wax in the ribbon well of the Imperial 66 in the Warden's Office.

LINK 3 — CONSCIOUSNESS OF GUILT (1998). The Duplicating Book: the Reprax counter advanced forty-one on 14 September against twelve logged, in a room whose keeper was nine miles away. The pathologist's estimate of eleven minutes between the fall and the emergency call. Box 17 standing on its shelf behind a timelock with no return entry against slip R98/2211, wearing a label typed on the Imperial 66 at full 'a' occlusion.

LINK 4 — IDENTITY (1998). The Warden's own Board of Dissolution working file: twenty-six Reprax copies of the contents of box 17, correctly foliated, correctly indexed, docketed the Ministry way on the outside third upside down to the tag — the habit Halvard Pike complained about in Wren's first hour and nobody has mentioned since — four of them copies of documents no longer in box 17. Twenty-six plus three copies of the accident report is twenty-nine. She copied the evidence, destroyed the originals and filed the copies, because destruction is the one act an archivist cannot perform.

LINK 5 — PRIOR KNOWLEDGE (1998). The used ribbon spool from the Imperial 66, preserved by the Cashier's stationery rule 4, on which the unsent sentence of 12 September — 'I know what you mean to send. Please do not send it.' — runs in unbroken sequence, with no ribbon change, directly into the accident report of 14 September. She has denied that knowledge in writing three times.

LINK 6 — SIGNATURE (1974). The p.p. sort: forty-eight documents from four independent custodies, of which every one of the forty-one dated 11 August to 3 November 1974 is per procurationem, and the seven outside that window are a genuine and shaky man's hand. Boundary dates 11 August and 18 November 1974, derived by the player unaided. Supported by the three refused oil requisitions R.741, R.748 and R.755; the struck-through despatch docket of 16 August; Works Order 75/188; and the memorandum to the Cashier of 6 November 1974.

LINK 7 — THE HAND HAS A NAME (1974). Absalom Ferrier could not have made those initials: Dr Munn's locum mileage claims from 12 August, Nurse Kilbride's visit ledger ('hemiplegic R side, no speech, cannot hold pen'), and the mirror offsets of the razored Order Book leaves. Only one other person in the building was authorised to sign per procurationem for the Warden, and the only document in 187 years in which she asserts she was here to do it is item 14 of the Authority's own schedule of liabilities: her superannuation claim for reckonable service from 1959, which the player crossed off in the first hour of Act I. Corroborated by the Rossport Inquiry's list of persons considered and not called, No. 33: 'Miss S. Ferrier — the Warden's private secretary — no official capacity — not called.'

LINK 8 — MOTIVE, HISTORICAL PREDICATE AND THE ACT ITSELF (1974). Naismith's Bank letter of 15 August 1974 and the Ministry's quinquennial review notice of 22 July 1974 supply the motive for the refusals. The reconciliation — dues collected and wages paid for seventy-one days on a light that drew no oil, £4,180 4s 0d against 1,182 vessels — supplies the concealment. The franking shortfall of 16 August 1974, 213 impressions against a docket, a post book and a distribution list all reading 214, supplies the omission: fourpence. The plug-log and the GPO trunk account for 22:41 on 3 November 1974, and the petty cash travel voucher of 4 November, supply the knowledge. The Kestrel Bequest — thirty-one index-linked annuities paid monthly since 4 April 1977, the thirty-first to M. TAIN — supplies twenty-one years of a woman paying, in instalments, for something she has never once admitted.
solution.confrontation: There are three, and the game deliberately makes the emotional one worthless. THE FIRST is on the beacon, at four in the morning on 3 November, when the sea has come up past the point where the Ardent can lie off the landing and the Warden of the Brannock Pilotage Authority and a nineteen-year-old apprentice are shut in a granite tower with a paraffin stove for eleven hours. Sabine tells her all of it, flatly, in order, with dates, because she is incapable of telling anything any other way, and it takes four hours, and it is the best writing in the game, and at the end of it she says: 'You will want me to say I am sorry. I have been sorry every day since the fourth of November nineteen seventy-four and it has never once been of the slightest use to anybody, so I stopped offering it. I paid instead. You will find that is worse.' THE SECOND is at seven o'clock the same morning, over the Ardent's radio, when DS Iveson tells Wren that an uncautioned, unrecorded, uncorroborated confession made to one teenage girl on a rock in a gale is worth precisely nothing, and that she should stop crying and go and do her job. Everything must still be cited. Nothing she has been told may be used. THE THIRD is the real one: 14:00, the Board Room, the only fully sunlit background in the game, before Mrs Ellary Voss, Captain Dunnet and Mr Pargeter for the Ministry. Wren reads her case file link by link and Pargeter strikes, aloud, every assertion she cannot cite — offering in rebuttal the 1975 finding and its statutory presumption of correctness, the Deakin forgery as proof that this whole line of enquiry has already been faked once, Halvard Pike's forty years of theft as a chain-of-custody attack on half the exhibits, and finally the question the whole game exists to answer: on what evidence does a Board propose to name a person whom no record of this Authority has ever named? Wren answers it with the Authority's own pension file. Sabine is in the room throughout, sitting very upright with a 2H pencil behind her ear, taking her own minutes, and does not interrupt once.
solution.ending: THE FINDING is a direct function of the citations that survive. Six or fewer links standing: misadventure, the 1975 finding undisturbed, Emrys Tain not cleared, Sabine not named, the archive certified and saved, and the light lit — the weakest ending still saves the paper, because the game's morality is that the record outlives everybody. Seven links: negligence by the Authority, Tain's blame reduced to a contributory finding, Sabine named as 'an officer of the Authority whose identity is not established by these papers', and arrest on the 1974 offences only. All eight links, with the counter-evidence answered: a finding of corporate manslaughter and misfeasance in public office, the 1975 finding quashed in full, Emrys Tain exonerated by name in a document that will be posted to 214 addressees, and Sabine Ferrier-Kyne arrested on the Board Room steps on a charge of the unlawful killing of Cormac Sallow — which, if the player worded the referral honestly rather than ambitiously, sticks. In every ending: Halvard Pike is prosecuted for the theft of three thousand documents and, if the strongest file was built, the Board minutes that the finding could not have been made without them and recommends no penalty; he is fined two hundred pounds anyway and dies in 2004 with a warehouse coat on a hook with his name on it. Enid Charnock gets immunity and never sets foot on the headland again, and her last words to the Board, by telephone, are 'I want it minuted that I raised it. Once. In writing.' Ottoline Verge is charged with nothing, and in the strongest ending asks to read the thirty-one names aloud and gets to fourteen. Rita Tain's forgery charge is dropped in the public interest on 11 January 1999. Ivo Sandbach is charged with theft and false accounting, his firm goes into administration on 19 January, and one Fresnel panel comes home. Bram Aylward's clients recover £9.1 million in 2003, of which the thirty-one families receive nothing, because they were never parties. AND IN EVERY SINGLE ENDING, WITHOUT EXCEPTION, TWO THINGS HAPPEN. At 23:04 on 3 November 1998 the Nine Bells shows three flashes in twenty seconds for the first time since 24 August 1974, visible from the Board Room window, from St Bride's churchyard, from Rossport quay and from Cardew, and nobody on that coast needs it explained to them. And Notice to Mariners 74/119 is issued at last — retyped from a scorched carbon, franked with a single fourpenny impression struck from the old die, entered in the register in its correct place with a note of the delay, and posted to all 214 addressees on Schedule D beginning with No. 1, the Keeper, Nine Bells Beacon — twenty-four years, two months and eighteen days late, with thirty-one names appended to it against Conservancy house style, at the insistence of a nineteen-year-old who will not be argued out of it. The last unscored choice in the game is whether Wren tells Rita Tain where thirty-four pounds a month has been coming from since 1977. The game does not grade it, does not comment on it, and ends on Rita's face, and then on the light.

subtitle: A Wren Adare Mystery
themes: A perfectly kept archive can be the most complete lie in the world, and the only cure for it is a stranger with a warrant and enough patience to read every line.
The culprit's crime and the culprit's grievance are the same fact: the institution's refusal to write a woman's name down was both the injury done to her and the mechanism of her impunity.
Bureaucratic omission is a form of violence with a price list. A notice not sent, a stamp not franked, a requisition refused pending refit — fourpence, and thirty-one lives.
Fair play is not a promise made by the author; it is an instrument the player operates. Any assertion that cannot be cited is struck, aloud, in front of you.

Truth is preserved by the wrong virtues. A thief's hoard, a cashier's petty economy, a developer's alibi diary and a machine too boring to bribe are what survive, while every honest, dutiful, correctly filed act of the institution is what buried it.
The honest witness is the most dangerous evidence there is: Norah Feaver told the exact truth for twenty-four years and nobody thought to ask her to count the seconds.

Everybody in this story arranged not to be asked. Ottoline typed her own name onto the list of witnesses not to be called; Sabine let a Charter do it for her. The difference between them is nerve, not kind — and the game refuses to tell you whether that is a difference at all.
Being right is not the same as being able to prove it, and Rita Tain has spent twenty-four years and every penny she owns learning the difference the expensive way.
timeline: 1811 — The Brannock Pilotage Authority is chartered to license pilots and levy dues on Ivory Sound. Article 9: 'The said office of Warden shall be holden by a man of full age.' Never amended.
1834 — The Nine Bells Beacon first exhibited on its reef, nine miles offshore.

1908 — A clockwork Fresnel optic is installed at the Nine Bells, character Fl(3) W 20s. In the same year a Kelvin & White stilling-well marigraph is installed in the north undercroft of Pilotage House and begins scratching the height of the sea onto a smoked drum.
1911 — Absalom Ferrier born. The Cadran Point light, nine miles SSE of the Nine Bells, is established with the character Fl(3) W 15s.
1919 — Cormac Sallow born. 1922 — Cass Verge born. 1926 — Ottoline (later Verge) born. 1932 — Halvard Pike born. 1935 — Enid Charnock born.
12 January 1940 — Sabine Ferrier born, only child of Absalom Ferrier and Isobel Ferrier.
1946 — The Warden's Order Book begins recording the closing hour of every working day; it will not miss one for fifty-two years.
1949 — Marguerite 'Rita' Tain born, daughter of the pilot Emrys Tain (b. 1926).
1954 — Halvard Pike joins the Authority as a copy boy, aged twenty-two.

1958 — Cormac Sallow appointed Lamp Superintendent. 1959 — Sabine Ferrier, aged nineteen, begins work as her father's unpaid private secretary; there is no post, no salary and no entry in the staff register.
1961 — Absalom Ferrier appointed Warden. An Imperial 66 typewriter is bought for the Warden's Office; its lower-case 'a' begins, imperceptibly, to fill with ink and wax.

1962 — Enid Charnock joins as junior cashier. 1968 — Ottoline Verge transfers to the Registrar's office and marries Cass Verge, relief keeper of the Nine Bells. Enid institutes stationery rule 4: no new typewriter ribbon to be issued until the used spool is returned.

22 July 1974 — The Ministry serves notice of a quinquennial review of pilotage authorities. An authority found to be without an effective Warden is to be abolished, its officers dismissed and its records dispersed.
9 August 1974 — Cormac Sallow makes his fortnightly visit to the Nine Bells and finds the No. 2 vaporiser cracked and the reserve oil down to ninety gallons.

SUNDAY 11 AUGUST 1974, c.16:00 — Absalom Ferrier suffers a cerebral haemorrhage at his desk in the Warden's Office. Sabine, aged thirty-four, finds him. He never signs anything again for ninety-nine days.

12 August 1974 — Sabine opens the Order Book and writes the first entry 'p.p. A. Ferrier' under Standing Order 4, which permits signature per procurationem in the Warden's temporary absence. She tells the Board chairman by telephone that her father has a chest infection. Dr Munn, locum, begins attending Brannock House, fourteen miles, twice weekly. Nurse Kilbride records: hemiplegic right side, no speech, cannot hold pen.
13 August 1974 — Sallow raises oil requisition R.741 for 400 gallons of paraffin for the Nine Bells and signs it.

15 AUGUST 1974 (Thursday) — Three things happen in one day. Naismith's Bank writes refusing any further facility: the Authority is approximately four months from insolvency. Sallow files his written report on the No. 2 vaporiser and the ninety gallons. And Sabine, on the Imperial 66 in the Warden's Office, drafts Notice to Mariners 74/119: MARINERS ARE ADVISED THAT THE LIGHT EXHIBITED FROM THE NINE BELLS BEACON MAY NOT BE RELIED UPON UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE. Two hundred and fourteen copies are run off on the Reprax 12; the impression counter advances 437 against 223 logged. The same afternoon, requisition R.741 is stamped REQUISITION NOT SANCTIONED — REFER WINTER REFIT and initialled p.p.

FRIDAY 16 AUGUST 1974 — Despatch day. On the contents docket for the fortnightly batch, Sabine rules 74/119 through in 2H pencil and initials the deletion p.p. The docket foot reads '214 @ 4d — £3 11s 4d'. The franking meter descends by £3 11s 0d: two hundred and thirteen impressions. One envelope is never franked and never posted — Schedule D No. 1, the Keeper, Nine Bells Beacon, care of the relief boatman, Cardew Post Office, telephone Cardew 4471. The 214 duplicated copies of the notice go into a japanned deed box on the strongroom bottom shelf; Sabine keeps one carbon in her personal file.

SUNDAY 18 AUGUST 1974 — Sabine defers Cass Verge's autumn residence at the beacon 'pending refit', with wages to continue, and instructs him in writing not to discuss it with the Lamp Superintendent or any other officer. The rock is empty. Verge is paid £18 4s 0d a week for eleven weeks — £200 4s 0d — to stay ashore, and begins drinking.
20 August 1974 — Cormac Sallow goes into Ilberry Cottage Hospital for a hernia operation. He is off duty until 10 October, which is why nobody with lamp knowledge is watching for seven weeks.

SATURDAY 24 AUGUST 1974, 21:10 — The last oil in the Nine Bells burns out. The keeper's log records: '22.10. No. 2 vapor. cracked. Oil out. Light down. Nothing more to be done here.' On the reverse of the last page, in pencil: tea, boot polish, a birthday card for Nan. The light will not be exhibited again for twenty-four years, two months and ten days.

24 August – 3 November 1974 — Seventy-one days. Ten complete dues weeks. One thousand one hundred and eighty-two vessels are charged £4,180 4s 0d in light dues for the Nine Bells. Wages are paid every week. No oil is drawn.
9 September 1974 — Oil requisition R.748 refused, REFER WINTER REFIT, initialled p.p.
12 September 1974 — The Cadran Point relief boatman reports 'Nine Bells not observed'. The report is minuted and carried to sundries.

7 October 1974 — Oil requisition R.755 refused, REFER WINTER REFIT, initialled p.p. Sallow, who signed it before his operation, is under anaesthetic when it comes back and never sees it; his file copy goes into a drawer at 3 Coastguard Row.
10 October 1974 — Sallow returns to duty, asks about the Nine Bells, is shown a wage sheet with the relief keeper paid and at station, and believes it. Cass Verge lies to his face.

SUNDAY 3 NOVEMBER 1974 — 22:34, the Rossport coastguard telephones extension 2, the Warden's Office, to ask whether the Nine Bells is exhibiting; a coaster queried it earlier in the evening. 22:41, an outgoing call from extension 2 to Cardew 4471, the public call box forty yards from Cass Verge's front door: four minutes, no answer. Verge is in the Ship Inn. 23:04, the coastal motor vessel Pelagia, inbound for Rossport with 118 aboard and Emrys Tain on the bridge, strikes the Nine Bells reef. Thirty-one people drown, among them Tain. 23:06 the coastguard relay, 23:11 the harbourmaster, 23:19 Rossport.
4 NOVEMBER 1974 — Sabine claims 3s 6d petty cash for a car to Cardew and back, 'urgent, on the Warden's instruction', and stands on Cass Verge's step. Neither of them ever speaks of it again.

6 November 1974 — A memorandum from the Warden's Office to the Cashier: the Nine Bells oil column is to be carried to Sundry Adjustments (Lights) pending refit. Initialled p.p. Enid Charnock keeps it, folded, inside the back cover of the cash book.
8 November 1974 — A relief keeper and 400 gallons of paraffin go out to the Nine Bells. Notice to Mariners 74/126 records the light as having been temporarily discontinued for repair.
18 NOVEMBER 1974 — Absalom Ferrier, partially recovered, signs his name for the first time in ninety-nine days. The p.p. stops. It is never used again in his lifetime.
31 December 1974 — Enid Charnock rules in a new column, 'Sundry Adjustments (Lights)', and carries £4,180 4s 0d into it. The balance will not move for ninety-six quarters.

February–June 1975 — The Rossport Inquiry, Sir Roderick Balgowan presiding. Cormac Sallow gives evidence on Day 9: 'The light was not discontinued', and 'I have no knowledge of any requisition being refused.' The first is true and misleading; the second is false and honest. Norah Feaver, aged nineteen, a survivor, testifies that she saw the light clearly, three flashes; nobody asks her to count the seconds. Ottoline Verge types the assessor's list of persons considered and not called, enters herself at No. 29 and ticks it. At No. 33: 'Miss S. Ferrier — the Warden's private secretary — no official capacity — not called.' FINDING: pilot error, on the strength of a hip flask recovered from a body. Emrys Tain is destroyed in print.

June 1975 — Works Order 75/188, 'seal chamber, damp': the Tide Room under the north undercroft is bricked up, with the marigraph, sixty-seven years of drums and the Inquiry's returned working papers inside it. The order is initialled p.p. — the last p.p. anyone ever writes in this building.

1975, autumn — Cass Verge, drunk, tells his wife the beacon was dark. He never mentions it again. Ottoline says nothing at the inquiry, because she is not called, and she has made sure of that herself.

1976 — Absalom Ferrier retires. Sabine is at last given a paid post: Clerk, Grade III. Rita Tain, aged twenty-seven, begins the campaign that will consume the rest of her life. Isobel Ferrier dies, leaving her daughter £41,000.

4 APRIL 1977 — Sabine settles the Kestrel Bequest through Mowbray & Slee of Rossport: a discretionary trust funded from her mother's legacy, paying thirty-one index-linked monthly standing orders to the dependants of the drowned. The thirty-first beneficiary is M. TAIN, who assumes for twenty-one years that the money is a legacy from her father's union and spends every penny of it on the campaign.

1979 — Absalom Ferrier dies. The Wardenship goes to Gethin Rowe. 1981 — Cass Verge dies, aged fifty-nine, without ever saying why he did not go out to the rock. 1984 — Cormac Sallow retires as Lamp Superintendent.

1985 — Ministry Circular 12/85 orders the Lights records destroyed on transfer of the beacon to Trinity House. Halvard Pike loads them into a van instead and takes them to a rented cottage at Cardew: the Oil Requisition Book 1966–1980, the Despatch Books 1970–79, the Lamp Superintendent's reports. He never opens them. They are filed under Lights, and he is a Pilotage man.

1989 — Two cover-ups happen in the same week and neither knows about the other. Sabine, now Deputy Warden, signs memorandum W/O 89/2 in her own name ordering the rationalisation and reboxing of series 14/B, and weeds seven documents; the leaves for 11 August–3 November are razored out of the Order Book at the gutter. Ottoline volunteers to redo the index and retypes forty-seven cards on the Underwood 5 to break the cross-references from the Nine Bells stores file to her husband's wage sheet. Sabine does not know what Ottoline is hiding. Ottoline believes she is protecting Absalom Ferrier.

1991 — Sabine Ferrier-Kyne is appointed Warden, aged fifty-one, thirty-two years after she started doing the job. Her husband dies the same year. Ottoline retires and comes back six days a week, unpaid.
1993 — The coast road washes out and is not rebuilt. Brannock Head is reached by ferry twice weekly, or by a causeway passable two hours either side of low water.
1996 — Rita Tain, refused legal aid for the fourth time and out of money, types the Deakin letter herself on an Adler Gabriele, ages it, and slips it into the lamp-room file.

1997 — The Coastal Services Act. The Brannock Pilotage Authority is dissolved with effect from 1 December 1998. Sandbach & Roule are engaged to convert Pilotage House into a heritage hotel, practical completion 1 December.

March 1998 — Sabine files a superannuation claim for reckonable service from 1959, £2,140 4s in dispute, because she needs the pension record clean before the Heritage Board appointment. It is the only document in existence in which she asserts that she was working in this building in 1974. It is entered as item 14 on the schedule of outstanding liabilities.

Early September 1998 — Sorting his retirement papers at 3 Coastguard Row, Cormac Sallow, seventy-nine, finds his file copy of requisition R.755 with the refusal initialled p.p., and recognises the hand. He tries to tell Rita Tain in August; she is too angry to listen.
8 September 1998 — Sallow requisitions series 14/B box 17 on slip R98/2198. The slip passes through the Warden's countersignature pigeonhole under Standing Order 7.

11 September 1998 (Friday) — Sallow posts a nine-line letter to the National Records Conservancy from Rossport, asking, with no explanation whatsoever, that 'series 14/B be read by a stranger before it leaves this building'.

12 September 1998 — On the Imperial 66, Sabine types: 'I know what you mean to send. Please do not send it. There is nothing in it that can help anybody now. S.' She does not post it. The sentence stays on the ribbon.

MONDAY 14 SEPTEMBER 1998 — 08:15, Halvard Pike takes the ferry to Rossport. 08:56, Sallow signs the visitors' book; the 'admitted by' column is initialled S.F-K. 09:10, he files slip R98/2211 for box 17 at a counter the Warden is working herself. c.09:40–10:24, they argue in the Muniment gallery north bay behind the map presses; he folds his spectacles and sets them on the reading slope. He refuses. She takes the folder; he takes hold of it; he goes backwards over baluster 3 of the north bay rail, recorded loose in the site diary since 2 September, and falls twenty-two feet onto flagstones. Death is instantaneous. She stands there for eleven minutes. 10:41, she telephones Rossport. 12:35, ambulance and police. That afternoon, while the building is in uproar, she runs twenty-nine impressions on the Reprax — twenty-six copies of the contents of box 17 and three of what she is about to type — removes four documents, relabels box 17 on the Imperial 66 and reshelves it behind the timelock. 16:50, she types the accident report and signs it Sabine Ferrier-Kyne, the first and only time in 187 years that her name appears on a record of this Authority. 17:40, the caretaker winds the gallery time-switch for the eleventh time that day.
15 September 1998 — The gallery rail is made good at the Warden's personal instruction, out of programme, no order number, not billed. Site diary item 63.

30 September 1998 — Inquest. Accidental death. 2 October 1998 — DS Marren Iveson requests the coroner's file on her own initiative, is told there is nothing in it, and puts her request slip back in the folder.

1 October 1998 — Sallow's letter, twice forwarded, reaches the National Records Conservancy. 3 October — Phyllida Halkett, Senior Appraiser, nominates Wren Adare. 6 October — Bram Aylward signs the Pilotage House visitors' book as 'Ministry, dissolution liaison', and begins photographing. 12 October — Halkett breaks her hip in a stairwell at the Ilberry store and lets everyone believe that is why an apprentice was sent. 20 October — Wren's commission is sealed under section 41.

MONDAY 26 OCTOBER 1998, 09:40 — Wren Adare lands at Brannock Head with nine days, a warrant, a loupe and a wire-bound casebook. 01:20 on the 27th, somebody burns paper in the courtyard incinerator; the damper was removed by scaffolders on 2 September and the flue will not draw; the rain puts it out badly.

27 October – 2 November 1998 — Nine days of paper. The scorched carbon. The card index gap. The strongroom and the flood. The Deakin letter and its collapse. Rita's arrest, 17:15 on 31 October. The revocation of Wren's commission, 16:20 on 1 November. The Tide Room. Pike's hoard and the reconciliation. The p.p. sort. Ottoline's biscuit tin. The switchboard. The ribbon. The fire at Cardew, 22:40 on 1 November. The Aldis lamp on the roof. And, at first light on 2 November, a crossing in a rising gale to a rock nine miles offshore.

2–3 NOVEMBER 1998 — Sabine Ferrier-Kyne and Wren Adare are shut in the Nine Bells Beacon by the weather for eleven hours, and at about four in the morning Sabine tells her everything, and it is worth nothing.

TUESDAY 3 NOVEMBER 1998 — The twenty-fourth anniversary. First light: the optic is repanelled, the sector plates set to three flashes in twenty seconds, the weight wound and the escapement set to release at 23:04. 14:00: the Board of Dissolution sits in the only sunlit room in the building, and strikes every assertion that cannot be cited. 23:04: the Nine Bells shows Fl(3) W 20s across nine miles of black water for the first time since 24 August 1974. And Notice to Mariners 74/119 is issued, franked with one fourpenny impression, to all 214 addressees on Schedule D, beginning with No. 1, the Keeper — twenty-four years, two months and eighteen days late, with thirty-one names appended.
title: NOTICE TO MARINERS
toneGuide:
THE GENRE ARGUMENT. This is not deduction from footprints; it is the auditor's fantasy. The player's superpower is literacy and stubbornness. Nothing is solved by intuition and everything is solved by cross-reference, and every single deduction is supported by a document the player can physically hold up to a window. The detective fantasy on offer is: I read it properly, and nobody else ever did.

PROSE REGISTER. Plain, cold, exact, and occasionally devastating by accident — the register of a good coroner's report. No purple. No 'suddenly'. The emotional beats land in numbers: fourpence; two hundred and thirteen impressions against two hundred and fourteen addressees; ninety-six quarters; thirty-one standing orders; eleven minutes. When something terrible happens, describe the paperwork it generated. The one place the prose is allowed to open out is on the water and inside the tower, and it should be noticeably shorter-breathed there, not longer.

WREN'S VOICE TIGHTENS UNDER FEAR. When she is calm she rambles slightly and corrects people's dates. When she is frightened she numbers her points. In the strongroom flood and on the crossing her casebook entries become telegraphic. Never write her as brave; write her as unable to stop working.

NOBODY IS A VILLAIN AND NOBODY IS EXEMPT. Every suspect is guilty of something real and none of the smaller crimes is the big one. The player must condemn Sabine and, in the boat coming back from the rock, understand precisely how it happened, and not be entirely certain they would have posted the notice either. Never let a character explain the theme aloud; the theme is the mechanic. If a line of dialogue states the meaning of the p.p., cut it.

THE THREE-STATE RULE (ART, MANDATORY). Every interior node is painted three times as the conversion eats the building: (A) intact and dust-sheeted, Acts I–II; (B) half-boxed, scaffold in, shelving stencilled LOT 4, Act III; (C) stripped to plaster, wires hanging, floor protected, Acts IV–V. Plus night variants for eleven key nodes. Returning to a room is never a visual repeat, the demolition schedule becomes a clock the player feels without a timer, and the archive visibly dies around the case as it is assembled. Rooms genuinely become unavailable on their scheduled dates.

SILHOUETTE DISCIPLINE. The judges' fair objection — twenty-six paintings of the same grey room — is answered by hard silhouette rules. The Nine Bells appears in Act II, not Act V: a hundred and twelve feet of granite through spray at four hundred yards, and the player is made to want it for two more acts. Every node must be identifiable at thumbnail by one non-negotiable shape: the tube head's brass octopus; the four hundred drawers as a wall of brass label-holders; the strongroom's three winding movements; the switchboard's twelve cords; the Reprax drum; the marigraph's glass stilling well; the incinerator's iron mouth; the churchyard's thirty-one slates; the signal mast; the optic. If two nodes can be confused at thumbnail, one of them is redesigned.

PALETTE. Wet slate and lead-grey granite; oxblood and bottle-green buckram spines; tobacco-cream foolscap and marbled endpapers; brass gone to verdigris; sodium amber; and one violent accent — the vermilion of the ISSUED stamp pad, which appears exactly seven times in the entire game and the seventh is on Notice to Mariners 74/119 on the last afternoon.

LIGHT. Low raking north light through twelve-foot sashes, thick with suspended dust: every registry background is a study in a shaft of grey daylight hitting paper. At night, isolated warm pools — the green banker's lamp, the microfilm reader's ground glass, a bare bulb swinging in the undercroft, a paraffin stove in a granite tower. The game walks steadily downward from four-o'clock October afternoon into the black hour before dawn on the rock, and then back up: the Board Room on 3 November is the only fully sunlit background in the game.

MATERIALS AND TEXTURE RULE. Dust sheets over ledger presses so the furniture reads as shrouded bodies; scaffold poles and translucent polythene the wind moves, so still backgrounds feel breathed on; japanned deed boxes stencilled with dead men's names; salt bloom flowering through limewash; mahogany, brass, bakelite, india rubber, sealing wax, cold paraffin. NO PEOPLE IN ANY BACKGROUND. Humanity appears only as objects left behind: a cup with the spoon still in it, spectacles folded on an open ledger, a cardigan over a chair, sheepskin slippers in drawer 388, thirty-one slate markers along a churchyard wall.

PORTRAIT RULE. Every living suspect is painted as a three-quarter oil against a dark ground in the manner of the Wardens' Hall portraits, so that the whole cast reads as already historical, already framed, already dead. Cormac Sallow, who is dead, is painted exactly the same way as everyone else, and so is Absalom Ferrier, whose caption on the Great Stair gives the dates of a Wardenship he was unconscious for a quarter of, and which the player passes forty times.

RHYTHM (THE VERB-MONOTONY FIX, NON-NEGOTIABLE). Head-work and hand-work alternate on a twenty-minute clock. No two consecutive puzzles may use the light table. Every act contains at least one beat in which something happens to a body rather than to a file: Act I the incinerator rake in the rain; Act II the timelock, the flood and the aborted crossing; Act III the crowbar on the bricked wall and re-hanging the marigraph; Act IV the fire, the roof mast and the crossing; Act V the optic. Every act contains at least one machine the player physically operates — franking meter, Reprax, timelock movements, switchboard, marigraph, Aldis lamp, clockwork optic — and at least one non-paper emotional object: the spectacles on the reading slope; the shopping list on the back of the last log page; the thirty-one slates along the churchyard wall; the smell of cold paraffin in a store nobody has opened in twenty-four years; a biscuit tin on a dresser.

SKILL CURVES (THE PLAYER MUST GET BETTER AT SOMETHING). Three named crafts, each taught in Act I on something trivial and each tested at rising difficulty in III, IV and V. (1) PAPER AUTHENTICATION — raking light for the watermark, chain-line count, fibre loupe, postmark gazetteer, ribbon-ink comparison; taught on Wren's own commission, kills the Deakin letter in Act III, proves the refused requisitions genuine in Act IV, and is defended under Board challenge in Act V. (2) TYPEWRITER FORENSICS — four machines with four sets of injuries, and the Imperial 66's progressively clogging 'a' as a dating curve. (3) SERIAL-RECORD AUDITING — counters, meters and registers: the franking meter, the Reprax counter, the time-switch, the GPO account, the reconciliation itself. A fourth, minor: ribbon-spool reading, taught as a party trick in Act I and lethal in Act IV.

HINTS ARE DIEGETIC AND OPINIONLESS. There is no hint system. There is a GPO call box on Rossport quay, reachable at low water with a pocketful of ten-pence pieces, and at the other end of it Phyllida Halkett will explain Conservancy procedure at any length, at any hour — what section 41 permits, how to certify a series, how to word an adverse report, what happens on 4 November — and will refuse, every single time, to have an opinion about the case. 'That's not a question for me.'

THE CASEBOOK IS THE GAME. Every assertion Wren records carries a citation column the player fills in. It is the evidence board, the requisition log, the specimen album and, in Act V, the case file itself. The Board of Dissolution strikes uncited assertions aloud, in front of the player, and the transcript prints with the gaps in it. This is not a fail state; it is a score, and it is the game's proof that it played fair.

NEW CASE PLUS. On completion, every 1974 document is unlocked from the start and the specimen bundle is available in the first thirty seconds. A second playthrough is not a faster playthrough; it is a different reading of the same text, which is the highest compliment a mystery can pay its audience. Achievement for finishing the game without ever once zooming to full resolution on the p.p. mark before Act IV: 'Per Procurationem'.

WHAT THIS GAME IS NEVER ALLOWED TO DO. No timers except the calendar. No fail states except a weak file. No chase sequences. No character explains the twist.
